en: Dawn is indeed the head of the sacrificial horse;

the sun is its eye, the wind its breath, and Vaiśvānara fire its open mouth. The year is the body of the sacrificial horse; heaven is its back, the intermediate space its belly, the earth its chest, the quarters its flanks, and the intermediate directions its ribs.
The seasons are its limbs, the months and half-months its joints, days and nights its foundation, the stars its bones, and the sky its flesh.
The undigested food in the stomach is the sands, the rivers are the intestines, and the mountains are the liver and lungs. The herbs and trees are its body hair;
the rising sun is its forepart, and the setting sun is its hindpart.
When it yawns, that is lightning;
when it shakes itself, that is thunder;
when it urinates, that is rain.
Speech indeed is his speech.
Day indeed was born as the greatness preceding the horse;
its source was in the eastern ocean. Night was born as the greatness following it.
Its source is in the other ocean.
These two, indeed, as the two forms of greatness (mahiman), have come into being on both sides of the horse:
having become a steed (haya), it carried the gods; as a prize-winner (vājī), the Gandharvas; as a racer (arvan), the Asuras; and as a horse (aśva), human beings.
The ocean alone is its kin; the ocean is its source.
In the beginning, there was nothing whatsoever here.
This [world] was indeed covered by death, which is hunger;
for hunger is death.
He made that mind [his own], thinking, "May I have a self.
He moved about performing fervor; from him, as he performed fervor, the waters were born.

"He indeed worshipped [the fire], thinking: 'May there be well-being (ka) for me. That is the very reason for the *arkya*'s name being *arka*. Well-being indeed comes to him who knows this reason for the *arkya*'s name being *arka*. — Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad 1.2.1.
The waters, indeed, are the *arka*.
That which was the foam of the waters solidified;
it became this earth.
He exerted himself in that [meditation].
From him, thus exhausted and heated, the essence of his vital energy emerged as fire.
He divided himself threefold: the sun as one third and the wind as one third.
This very breath is thus distributed threefold.
Of it, the eastern direction is the head, and those two [celestial bodies] are the two arms.
Now, the western quarter is its tail; that [northern] and that [southern] are its two thighs; the southern and the northern are its two sides;
heaven is its back, the intermediate space its belly, and this earth its chest.
This very [Self] is established in water;
wherever it goes, it becomes established there—so it is for one who knows thus.
He desired: "May a second self be born to me.
Through his mind, he entered into union with speech—[he who is] hunger, death.
That which was the seed became the year.
Before that, there was no year.
He bore him for as long as a year;
after that length of time, he brought him forth.
When he was born, he opened his mouth wide;
he made a sound, and that became speech. (Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad 1.2.4)
He thought, "If I were to destroy this [world], I would make food less.
With that speech and with that self, he created all this—whatever there is: the Ṛg-verses, the Yajus-formulas, the Sāman-chants, the meters, the sacrifices, progeny, and cattle.
Whatever he created, he resolved to eat.
Or, she eats everything; that is the Aditi-nature of Aditi.
He who knows this Aditi-nature of Aditi becomes the eater of all, and everything becomes his food. (Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad 1.2.5)
He desired: "May I sacrifice again with a greater sacrifice. He exerted himself;
he practiced austerity.
As he was exhausted and tormented, his fame and vigor departed;
for fame and vigor are indeed the vital breaths.
When those vital breaths had departed, his body began to swell.
His mind was fixed on his body alone.
He desired: "May this be fit for sacrifice for me; may I be possessed of this through my own self.
From that, the horse came into being. Because it moved (*aśvat*), it became fit for sacrifice (*medhya*); that is precisely why the Horse Sacrifice is called *Aśvamedha*.
He indeed knows the Aśvamedha who knows it thus. He considered that [sacrifice] as not yet fully secured; therefore, at the end of the year, he offered it as a victim for himself.
He drove the animals away from the deities;
therefore, they offer an animal sprinkled for all the deities as belonging to Prajāpati.
This indeed is the Aśvamedha, which shines yonder.
The year is its self;
this fire is the Arka;
these worlds are its selves.
These two, the Arka and the Aśvamedha,
are but one deity, namely Death itself;
he conquers recurrent death.
Death does not reach him;
death becomes his very self;
he attains a full lifespan.
He becomes one with these deities. (Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad 1.2.7)
There were two classes of Prajāpati’s offspring: the gods and the asuras. Of these, the gods were fewer, while the asuras were more numerous. They contended with one another for these worlds.
Then the gods said, "Come, let us overcome the asuras at the sacrifice by means of the Udgītha. (Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad 1.3.1)
They said to Speech, "Do you sing the Udgītha for us.
"So be it," Speech replied, and she sang the Udgītha for them.
Whatever enjoyment is in speech, that she sang for the gods.
Whatever good he spoke, he did for himself; they realized, "By this Udgātṛ priest, they will surpass us," and rushing toward him, they pierced him with evil.
That which is evil is this very thing that one speaks when speaking what is improper;
that indeed is that evil.
Then they said to Prāṇa, "Sing the Udgītha for us. "So be it," Prāṇa replied; he sang the Udgītha for them.
Whatever enjoyment there is in Prāṇa, that he obtained for the gods by singing.
Whatever good they smelled, that they attributed to themselves; they knew, "By this Udgātṛ,
they will surpass us," and having rushed at him, they pierced him with evil.
That which is evil is precisely that which one smells here as something disagreeable;
that indeed is that evil.
Then they said to the eye, "Sing the Udgītha for us. "So be it," [replied] the eye; it sang the Udgītha for them.
Whatever enjoyment was in the eye, that it sang forth for the gods.
Whatever good he saw, he directed toward himself.
They realized, "By this Udgātṛ priest, they will surpass us.
They rushed at him and pierced him with evil.
That which is this evil is precisely that which one sees here as unseemly;
it is that very same evil.
Then they said to the ear, "Sing the Udgītha for us. "So be it," [it replied]. For them, the ear sang the Udgītha.
Whatever enjoyment was in the ear, that it sang for the gods.
Whatever auspicious thing he heard, he took for himself.
They realized, "By this Udgātṛ priest, they will surely surpass us.
They rushed toward him and pierced him with evil.
That which is this evil is simply that which one hears here as discordant;
that indeed is that evil.
Then they said to the mind, "Do you sing the Udgītha for us.
"So be it," [said] the mind; it sang the Udgītha for them.
Whatever enjoyment is in the mind, that it sang for the gods.
Whatever good he intended for himself,
they perceived it and, thinking, "By this Udgātṛ priest they will surpass us," they rushed at him and pierced him with evil.
That which is evil is this very thing that one conceives as improper;
that indeed is that evil.
In this very way, they indeed afflicted these deities with evils;
in this very way, they pierced them with evil.
Then they said to this breath in the mouth, "Do you sing the Udgītha for us.
"So be it," [replied] that breath; for them, this breath sang the Udgītha.
They perceived: "Verily, with this as our singer, they will overcome us."
They rushed at him, intending to pierce him with evil.
But just as a clod of earth would shatter upon hitting a stone, even so they shattered and perished, scattering in all directions.
Thereupon the gods prevailed, and the Asuras were defeated.
He prospers in himself, and his hateful rival comes to ruin—he who knows thus. BrhUp 1.3.7.
They said, "Where indeed was he who thus attached himself to us?
"He was here within the mouth," they replied. He is Ayāsya Āṅgirasa, for he is the essence (rasa) of the limbs (aṅga).
This deity is indeed named "the Far-off" (dūṛ), for death is far from her. And death becomes far from him who knows this. Br̥hadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad 1.3.9.
That deity, having struck away the evil—death—from these deities, sent it to where the end of these quarters is;
there he deposited their evils.
Therefore, one should not go to a crowd, nor should one go to the end [of the quarters], lest one fall into evil—death.
Verily, that deity, having struck away the evil of death from these deities, then carried them beyond death.
She indeed carried speech across first.
When it was released from death, it became fire.
This very fire, having transcended death, shines beyond it. (Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad 1.3.12)
Then he carried the vital breath (prāṇa) across. When it was released from death, it became the wind.
This very wind, having transcended death, blows beyond it.
Then the eye carried it across.
When it was released from death, it became the sun.
That very sun, having transcended death on the far side, shines.
Then he carried the ear across.
When it was liberated from death, it became the quarters.
These quarters have transcended death on the far side.
Then the mind carried it across. When it was released from death, it became the moon.
That very moon shines, having transcended death on the far side.
In this very way, indeed, this deity carries him across death, who knows thus. (Br̥hadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad 1.3.16)
Then he sang for himself the song for the sake of food.
For whatever food is eaten here, it is eaten by him alone; thus he becomes established in this world.
Those gods said:
"All this that exists is indeed food; you have sung for yourself as much as that."
"Partake of this food with us," he said.
"Then enter into me," they replied.
"So be it," he said; and they entered into him on all sides.
Therefore, whatever food he eats, by that these [deities] are satisfied.
Thus indeed do his own people gather around him who knows this—he becomes the supporter of his own, the best, the leader, the eater of food, and the sovereign.
But whoever among his own people seeks to oppose one who knows this, he is not at all capable of supporting those dependent on him.
Now, he who experiences this, or who desires to support dependents by means of this, is indeed capable of supporting his dependents.
He is Ayāsya Āṅgirasa, for he is the essence (*rasa*) of the limbs; indeed, the vital breath (*prāṇa*) is the essence of the limbs,
for the vital breath is truly the essence of the limbs.
Therefore, from whichever limb the vital breath (prāṇa) departs, that very limb withers;
for this indeed is the essence of the limbs.
He is indeed Bṛhaspati.
Vāc is the Bṛhatī;
he is her lord, and therefore he is Bṛhaspati.
He indeed is Brahmaṇaspati.
Speech is indeed Brahman;
he is its lord, therefore he is Brahmaṇaspati.
This very one is indeed the *sāman*.
Speech is indeed the *sāman*, for it is both "she" (*sā*) and "he" (*ama*); that is the essence of the *sāman*'s name.
Furthermore, because he is equal to a flea, equal to a mosquito, equal to an elephant, equal to these three worlds, and equal to this entire universe—for that reason also he is the *sāman*.
He who knows this Sāman thus attains union with and residence in the same world as the Sāman. (Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad 1.3.22)
This, indeed, is the Udgītha.
Breath is "ut," for by breath all this is upheld;
speech alone is "gīthā."
And because it is sung loudly (*uccair gīyate*), it is the *udgītha*. Thus, it is the *udgītha*.
Moreover, on this point Brahmadatta Caikitāneya, while consuming the King [Soma], said:
"May this King strike off the head of that man who sang the Udgītha for Ayāsya Āṅgirasa by means other than this!
For he indeed sang the Udgītha by means of speech and breath alone.
Whoever knows the property of this very Sāman, his becomes property.
Its property, indeed, is its tone (*svara*).
Therefore, one who is about to perform the office of a priest should seek a tone in his speech.
One should perform the priestly office with speech endowed with the correct tone (*svara*).
Therefore, at a sacrifice, people desire to see one who possesses the correct tone;
moreover, it belongs to him who has it.
He indeed possesses his own property who thus knows this property of the Sāman.
He who knows the gold of this very Sāman obtains gold.
Indeed, its gold is its tone;
he who thus knows this gold of the Sāman obtains gold.
He who knows the support of this very Sāman becomes firmly established.
Verily, speech is its support;
for it is in speech that this Prāṇa is established when it is sung.
"Food," so indeed some say. (Br̥hadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad 1.3.27)
Now, therefore, follows the ascending of the *pavamāna* chants.
The *prastotṛ* indeed intones the *sāman*;
when he is about to intone it, he should mutter these [formulas].
"Lead me from unbeing to being; lead me from darkness to light; lead me from death to immortality."

When he says, "Lead me from non-existence to existence," non-existence is death and existence is immortality; thus he says, "Lead me from death to immortality, make me immortal. When he says, "Lead me from darkness to light," [the same applies].
"Death is indeed darkness; light is immortality. 'Lead me from death to immortality; make me immortal'—this is what he says.
'Lead me from death to immortality':
there is nothing here that is obscure."
Now, regarding those other hymns, he should sing for himself the obtainment of food therein;
therefore, in those [hymns], he should choose a boon—
whatever desire he may wish for.

This very Udgātṛ priest, knowing thus, sings for himself or for the sacrificer whatever desire he may desire. This, indeed, is the conquest of the worlds. For one who knows this Sāman thus, there is no hope of not attaining the light of heaven.
In the beginning, this was indeed the Self alone, in the form of a person.
He looked around and saw nothing other than himself.
He first uttered, "I am."
From that, "I" (aham) became his name.
Therefore even now, when addressed, he first says "This is I" (ayam aham), and then pronounces whatever other name he may have.
Because he burnt away all evils before all this [universe], he is therefore called *puruṣa*.
He who knows this indeed consumes him who desires to be before him. (Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad 1.4.1)
He was afraid; therefore, one who is alone is afraid. He then reflected: "Since there is nothing else besides me, of what am I afraid?"
From that very moment his fear departed.
For of what could he have been afraid? Indeed, it is from a second that fear arises.
He indeed did not find delight;
therefore, one who is alone does not find delight.
He desired a second.
He was of such a size as that of a man and a woman in close embrace.
He caused this very self of his to fall apart into two parts;
from that, there came to be a husband and a wife.
"Therefore," said Yājñavalkya, "this [body] is like a half-egg-shell.
Therefore, this space is filled by a woman.
He united with her.
From that, human beings were born.
She reflected thus: "How indeed can he procreate after having produced me from himself?
Well, let me disappear.
She became a cow, and the other became a bull.
He united with her;
from that, cattle were born.
One became a mare, the other a stallion.
The she-ass was one, the male donkey was the other; he united with her, and from that the single-hoofed animal was born.
One became a goat, the other a he-goat;
one became a sheep, the other a ram. He united with her.
From that, goats were born.
In this very way, he created everything whatsoever that exists in pairs, down to the ants.
He realized: "I indeed am the creation, for I have created all this. From that, he became the creation (Sṛṣṭi). He who knows this becomes part of this creation of his. (Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad 1.4.5)
Then he rubbed [the fire-sticks] together; from his mouth and from his hands he created fire.
Therefore, these two [parts] are hairless on the inside.
For the womb within is indeed hairless.
Thus, when they say, "Sacrifice to this one, sacrifice to that one," sacrificing to each individual deity is actually the emission of this very [Self];
for he alone is all the gods.
Then, whatever here is moist, that he created from semen;
that, indeed, is Soma.
For all this world is just this much: food and the eater of food.
Soma indeed is the food, and Agni is the eater of food.

This is the "excessive creation" (atisṛṣṭi) of Brahman: that he created the gods who are superior; and because, though being mortal himself, he created those who are immortal, it is therefore called the "excessive creation."
He who knows this becomes one who has full authority over this [earth]. Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad 1.4.6.
At that time, this world was indeed undifferentiated;
it was differentiated by name and form alone, [in the sense] "this one has such a name, he has such a form.
Even now, this world is likewise differentiated by name and form alone, [in the sense] "this one has such a name, he has such a form."
This very [Self] has entered here up to the tips of the fingernails, just as a razor might be placed in a razor-case, or as fire in a nest of fire-wood.
They do not see it, for it is incomplete; only when breathing does it become what is called "breath."
When speaking, it is speech; when seeing, it is the eye; when hearing, it is the ear; when thinking, it is the mind.
These are merely names for its functions.
He who venerates any one of these individually does not truly know it.
For this [Self] is incomplete when considered through any one of these [aspects] individually; therefore, one should worship it simply as "the Self" (ātman). For in this [Self], all these become one.
This very Self is the track of all this;
for by means of it one knows all this.
Just as one might find [lost cattle] by means of a footprint, so does he who knows this find fame and renown. (Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad 1.4.7)
This very Self is dearer than a son, dearer than wealth, dearer than everything else—this Self which is more internal.
If someone were to say to one who declares anything other than the Self to be dear, "He will lose what is dear," it would likely come to pass exactly so.
Therefore, one should worship the Self alone as dear.
He who venerates the Self alone as dear—verily, his dear ones do not perish.

Regarding this they say: "What indeed was that Brahman which, knowing it, men think they shall become everything through the knowledge of Brahman? What was that Brahman by which all this came to be? (Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad 1.4.9)
In the beginning, this was indeed Brahman.
It knew only itself:
"I am Brahman."
Therefore, all that came into being.
Whosoever among the gods awakened to that, he alone became that;
likewise among the seers.
The same applies to human beings.
Seeing this, the seer Vāmadeva realized: "I was Manu, and I was the Sun.
Even today, whoever knows this—"I am Brahman"—becomes all this.
Indeed, not even the gods have power over one who has attained this,
for he becomes their very self.
But he who worships another deity, thinking, "He is one and I am another," does not know.

As is a beast, so is he to the gods. Just as many beasts serve a man, even so does each individual person serve the gods. When even a single beast is taken away, it is unpleasant; how much more so when many are?
Therefore, that which humans might know is not dear to them.
In the beginning, this was indeed Brahman alone, one only. Being one, it did not flourish. It emitted from itself that superior form, the Kṣatra.
Those which are these sovereignties among the gods— Indra, Varuṇa, Soma, Rudra, Parjanya, Yama, Mṛtyu, and Īśāna—
from that sovereignty there is nothing higher.
Therefore, in the Rājasūya sacrifice, the Brāhmaṇa sits below the Kṣatriya and worships him.
He thus bestows that glory upon the *kṣatra* alone.
This *brahman* is the womb of the *kṣatra*;
therefore, even if a king attains the highest position, he finally resorts to the *brahman* as his own womb.
But he who injures him goes to his own source;
he becomes worse, just as one who has harmed a superior.
He did not multiply at all.
He created the Viś.
Those classes of divine beings that are enumerated in groups are these: the Vasus, the Rudras, the Ādityas, the Viśvedevas, and the Maruts.
He did not multiply at all;
he created the Śūdra caste, Pūṣan.
This earth, indeed, is Pūṣan.
For this indeed nourishes all this, whatever there is here.
It did not flourish.
It emitted from itself that form which is superior: Dharma.
This Dharma is the sovereign power (kṣatra) of sovereign power.
Therefore, there is nothing superior to dharma.
Thus, even one who is weak relies upon dharma to prevail over the strong,
just as one does with a king.
That which is indeed Dharma is truth;
therefore, they say of one who speaks truth that he speaks Dharma,
and of one who speaks Dharma that he speaks truth.
For this indeed becomes both of these.
This is the Brahmin, the Kṣatriya, the Vaiśya, and the Śūdra.
Among the gods, it became the Brahman through Agni alone; among humans, it became the Brāhmaṇa, and through the Kṣatriya, the Kṣatriya.
A Vaiśya [attains his goal] through a Vaiśya, and a Śūdra through a Śūdra.
Therefore, among the gods they desire a world in fire alone, and among humans, in a Brāhmaṇa.
For it was through these two forms that Brahmā came into being.

Now, whoever departs from this world without having seen his own world, it does not benefit him, being unknown to him—just as a Veda that has not been studied or another rite that has not been performed.
Even if such a person who lacks this knowledge performs a great meritorious deed, it indeed perishes for him in the end.
One should worship the Self alone as the world.
He who worships the Self alone as the world—his work is never exhausted;
for from this very Self he creates whatever he desires. (Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad 1.4.15)
Moreover, this very self is the world of all beings.
In that he offers oblations and performs sacrifices, by that it is the world of the gods;
and in that he recites the formulas, by that it is the world of the seers.
Now, in that he offers to the ancestors, and in that he desires offspring, by that it belongs to the ancestors;
then, in that he provides lodging for men and gives them food, by that it belongs to men;
then, in that he finds grass and water for the animals, by that it belongs to the animals.
Inasmuch as wild beasts, birds, and even ants subsist upon what is in his house, by that [act] their world is secured for him.
Just as one would surely desire safety for one's own world,
even so do all beings always desire safety for one who knows this.
This, indeed, has been understood and investigated.
In the beginning, this universe was the Self alone, just one.
He desired: "May I have a wife; then may I procreate.
May I have wealth; then may I perform ritual action."

This indeed is the extent of desire: even if one were to seek, one would not find anything more than this. Therefore, even now, a person living alone desires: "May I have a wife, and may I procreate; may I have wealth, and may I perform ritual acts."
As long as he does not attain even one of these, he considers himself incomplete;
his completeness consists in this:
the mind alone is his self.
Speech is the wife;
breath is the offspring;
the eye is human wealth.
For one finds that with the eye;
the ear is divine,
for one hears that with the ear.
The self alone is his action;
for by means of the self one performs action.
This very sacrifice consists of five parts.
The animal is fivefold; man is fivefold;
all this that exists here is fivefold.
He who knows this obtains all this. Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad 1.4.17.
When the Father produced the seven foods by means of wisdom and austerity, he made one common to all; he assigned two to the gods;
he set three aside for himself; and he gave one to the animals.
In that everything is established—both that which breathes and that which does not.
Why is it that these do not perish, even though they are being consumed all the time? He who knows that imperishability eats food with his very face.
"He goes even unto the gods; he lives upon strength"—thus are the verses. (Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad 1.5.1)
"When the Father produced the seven kinds of food by means of wisdom and austerity"— for the Father did indeed produce them by means of wisdom and austerity— "one of these is common to all.
This very food which is eaten here is that one which is common to all.
He who venerates this does not turn away from evil, for this is mixed. It is said:
"It assigned two [shares] to the gods."
There is the *huta* and the *prahuta*.
Therefore, they offer oblations to the gods and offer them forth.
Moreover, they say it refers to the New and Full Moon sacrifices (*darśapūrṇamāsa*).
Therefore, one should not be a frequent performer of the *iṣṭi* sacrifice.
"He gave one [part] to the animals"—
that was milk.
For indeed, humans and animals subsist on milk first.
Therefore, when a boy is born, they first cause him to lick clarified butter or suckle him at the breast.
Then, regarding a calf that has been born, they say, "From grass."
Upon that everything is established—both that which breathes and that which does not.
For upon milk indeed all this is established, both that which breathes and that which does not.
Regarding this, they say: "One who offers milk as an oblation for a year overcomes repeated death."
One should not understand it thus:
on whatever day one offers the oblation, on that very day one who knows this conquers recurrent death,
for he bestows all food upon the gods.
Why is it that these [foods] are not exhausted, even though they are being consumed all the time? Or rather, the Person (puruṣa) is the imperishable one;
for he produces this food again and again.
"He who knows this imperishable one"—
the person indeed is the imperishable one,
for he produces this food through every act of thought by means of his ritual works.
If one were not to perform this, he would indeed perish.
"He eats food with his face"—the face is the *pratīka*; thus, it means "with the mouth."
"He goes to the gods; he lives upon strength"—this is the praise. (Br̥hadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad 1.5.2)
"He made three for himself":
namely mind, speech, and breath; these he made for himself.
"I was elsewhere in mind, I did not see; I was elsewhere in mind, I did not hear"—for it is with the mind alone that one sees, and with the mind that one hears.
Desire, volition, doubt, faith, lack of faith, steadfastness, lack of steadfastness, shame, intelligence, and fear—all these are nothing but the mind.
Therefore, even when touched from behind, one discerns it by means of the mind.
Whatever sound there is, that is speech alone.
For this [life] depends on the end; for this is not [independent]. Prāṇa, apāna, vyāna, udāna, and samāna—all this is indeed prāṇa.
This self, verily, consists of that.
Consisting of speech, consisting of mind, and consisting of breath.
These three worlds are these very [three]:
speech is this world, mind is the intermediate world, and breath is yonder world.
These indeed are the three Vedas:
speech is the Ṛgveda, the mind is the Yajurveda, and the breath is the Sāmaveda.
The gods, the ancestors, and humans are these very ones:
speech indeed is the gods, the mind is the ancestors,
and the vital breath is humans.
The father, the mother, and the offspring—these indeed exist.
Mind is the father, speech is the mother, and breath is the offspring.
The known, the object of inquiry, and the unknown— these alone are it.
Whatever is known is a form of speech,
for speech is the knower.
Speech, having become that, protects him.
Whatever is to be known through inquiry, that has the nature of the mind;
for the mind is indeed that which is to be known through inquiry.
Having become that, the mind protects him.
Whatever is unknown is the form of the vital breath (prāṇa),
for the vital breath is indeed unknown.
Having become that, the vital breath protects him.
Of that speech, the earth is the body and this fire is its form as light. As great as speech is, so great is the earth, and so great is this fire.
Now, heaven is the body of this mind;
that sun is its form of light.
As far as the mind extends, so far extends heaven, and so great is that sun.
The two united as a pair;
from that, the vital breath was born;
he is Indra.
This very one is without a rival.
A second is indeed a rival. He who knows this has no rival. (Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad 1.5.12)
Now, water is the body of this vital breath;
that moon is its form of light. As great as the vital breath is, so great are the waters, and so great is that moon.
All these [worlds] are indeed equal and all are infinite.
He who worships them as finite wins a finite world;
but he who worships them as infinite wins an infinite world. (Br̥hadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad 1.5.13)
This very year, Prajāpati, consists of sixteen parts;
its fifteen parts are the nights,
and its sixteenth part is the constant one.

It is filled by the nights and it wanes by the nights. On the night of the new moon, having entered into all these living beings by means of this sixteenth part, it is born again in the morning from there.
Therefore, on that night, one should not deprive any living being of its life, even a lizard, out of reverence for this very deity.
That Prajāpati who is the year, consisting of sixteen parts, is indeed this person who knows thus;
his wealth constitutes fifteen parts,
while his self alone is his sixteenth part.
It is filled by wealth alone and it is depleted by wealth alone.
This self is the nave,
and wealth is the felly.
Therefore, even if one loses everything, if he lives by himself, they say, "He has escaped with the rim. (Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad 1.5.15)
Now, there are indeed three worlds: the world of men, the world of the fathers, and the world of the gods.
This world of men is to be won by a son alone, and not by any other rite;
the world of the fathers is won by rites.
Through knowledge, one attains the world of the gods.
Indeed, the world of the gods is the best of all worlds;
therefore, they praise knowledge.
Now, therefore, follows the transmission.
When he thinks he is about to depart, he says to his son: "You are the Brahman, you are the sacrifice, you are the world.
The son replies: "I am the Brahman, I am the sacrifice, I am the world."
Whatever has been recited, all that is unified in "Brahman";
whatever sacrifices there are, all those are unified in "Sacrifice";
whatever worlds there are, all those are unified in "World."
"This whole world is just this much;
let him not, being all this, consume [us] from here.
Therefore, they say that a son who has been instructed is "worldly" (lokya).
Therefore, he instructs him.
When one who knows this departs from this world, he enters into his son together with these very vital breaths (*prāṇa*).
Whatever has been done by him (the father) improperly, from all that the son releases him; therefore he is called "son" (*putra*).
Through his son alone he finds firm support in this world;
then these immortal deities, the vital breaths, enter into him.
Then divine speech enters him from the earth and from Agni.
That indeed is divine speech by which whatever one says comes to be exactly so.
From the day and from the sun, the divine mind enters him.
That indeed is the divine mind by which one becomes truly blissful and does not grieve.
And from the waters and from the moon, the divine breath enters him.
That indeed is the divine breath which, whether moving or not moving, neither suffers nor is harmed.
He who knows this becomes the self of all beings.
As is this deity, so is he;
as all beings protect this deity, even so do all beings protect one who knows this.
Whatever these creatures grieve for, that becomes his grief alone.
Only merit goes to him;
indeed, evil does not go to the gods.
Now, therefore, follows the investigation of vows.
Prajāpati created ritual actions;
once created, they vied with one another.
"I shall speak," thus the voice resolved;
"I shall see," thus the eye;
"I shall hear," thus the ear.
In this way, he exhausted other actions according to their nature;
Death, becoming weariness, took possession of them and overcame them.
Having reached them, Death seized hold of them;
therefore, speech indeed becomes exhausted,
and the eye becomes exhausted.
The ear grew weary;
yet it did not reach this very one, which is the central breath (prāṇa).
They resolved to know them.
"This one is indeed the best among us, for whether moving or not moving, he neither trembles nor suffers harm. Come now, let us all become his very form. They all became his very form.
Therefore, they are called by this name, "the vital breaths" (prāṇāḥ). Indeed, the family in which one who knows this is born is called by that very name.
And whoever competes with one who knows thus withers away.
"Having finally withered away, he indeed dies"—this is with reference to the self (adhyātma).
Now, with respect to the deities: "I shall indeed blaze," so Agni resolved;
"I shall burn," so Āditya [resolved].
"I shall speak," says the moon;
likewise do the other deities, each according to its own nature.
Just as the middle vital breath among these vital breaths, so is Vāyu among these deities.
For other deities set, but not Vāyu;
this deity, Vāyu, is indeed one that never sets.
Now, there is this verse:
"From where the sun rises and where it sets"—
it indeed rises from the vital breath (prāṇa) and sets in the vital breath.
"The gods established that as the law: 'That very same [law] holds today and it shall hold tomorrow.
Whatever these [gods] undertook yesterday, that very same thing they do today.
Therefore, one should observe only a single vow: one should both breathe out and breathe in."
"Let not the evil, death, overtake me"—
if he should practice [this], desiring to complete it, he thereby wins union with and residence in the same world as that deity.
This world consists of three things: name, form, and action.
Of these names, speech is their *uktha*;
for from it all names arise.
This is their *sāman*;
for this is equal with all names. This is their *brahman*.
For this indeed bears all names.
Now, among forms, the eye is their *uktha*;
for from it all forms arise.
It is their *sāman*.
For this is equal to all forms; this is the Brahman of these [forms]. For this indeed sustains all forms. (Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad 1.6.2)
Now, "the self of actions"— this is their *uktha*,
for from it all actions arise;
this is their *sāman*.
For this is equal to all ritual acts;
this is their Brahman,
for it sustains all ritual acts.
These three, being existent, are this one Self;
this one Self, being existent, is these three. This very immortal is covered by truth.
Breath indeed is the immortal;
name and form are the real.
By these two, this breath is concealed.
There was once a proud Gārgya, a learned man of the Bālāki clan.
He said to Ajātaśatru of Kāśī, "I shall tell you about Brahman.
Ajātaśatru replied, "We shall give a thousand [cows] for such a speech as this."
"Janaka, Janaka," indeed people are running about, saying. (Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad 2.1.1)
Gārgya said: "The person who is there in the sun—that is precisely the one I venerate as Brahman.
Ajātaśatru replied: "Do not talk to me about him!
I venerate him rather as the one who stands over all beings, the head, the king."
He who venerates him thus becomes pre-eminent, the head and king of all beings.
Gārgya said: "The person who is there in the moon—that very one I worship as Brahman.
Ajātaśatru said: "Do not talk to me about him!
I worship him rather as the Great One, clad in white, King Soma."
He who venerates it thus—day after day, his [Soma] is pressed and poured out;
his food is never exhausted.
Gārgya said: "The person who is there in lightning—that very one I meditate upon as Brahman.
Ajātaśatru said: "Do not talk to me about him!
I meditate upon him rather as 'the radiant one'."
He who venerates him thus becomes radiant,
and his offspring becomes radiant.
Gārgya said: "The person who is right here in space—that is the one I venerate as Brahman.
Ajātaśatru said: "Do not talk to me about him!
I venerate him rather as the 'Full' that does not move."
He who venerates him thus is filled with offspring and cattle; his progeny does not perish from this world.
Gārgya said: "The person who is here in the wind—that very one I worship as Brahman.
Ajātaśatru said: "Do not converse with me about him!
I worship him rather as Indra Vaikuṇṭha, the unconquered army."
He who venerates him thus becomes victorious, unconquerable, and a vanquisher of his enemies.
Gārgya said: "The person who is here in the fire—that is the one I worship as Brahman.
Ajātaśatru said: "Do not talk to me about him! I worship him rather as 'the overcomer' (viṣāsahiḥ)."
He who meditates upon him thus becomes a conqueror;
his offspring, indeed, become conquerors.
Gārgya said: "The person who is here in the water—that very one I worship as Brahman.
Ajātaśatru said: "Do not talk to me about him!
I worship him rather as 'the Counterpart' (pratirūpa)."
He who venerates him thus—verily, only what is suitable approaches him, and not what is unsuitable;
moreover, from him is born one who is suitable.
Gārgya said: "The person who is here in the mirror—that very one I worship as Brahman.
Ajātaśatru said: "Do not talk to me about him!
I worship him rather as 'the Radiant' (rociṣṇu)."
He who venerates him thus becomes radiant;
his offspring become radiant;
and so too do those with whom he comes into contact.
He outshone them all.
Gārgya said: "This very one who, as a person walks along, follows behind him making a sound—that is the one I venerate as Brahman.
Ajātaśatru said: "Do not talk to me about him!
I venerate him rather as 'Life' (asu)."
He who venerates it thus attains a full lifespan in this world;
his vital breath does not leave him before the appointed time.
Gārgya said: "The person who is here in the quarters—him indeed I worship as Brahman.
Ajātaśatru said: "Do not talk to me about him!
I worship him rather as the 'Second' and the 'Inseparable'."
He who venerates him thus becomes possessed of a companion;
his group is never separated from him.
Gārgya said: "This very person who consists of shadow—that is the one I venerate as Brahman.
Ajātaśatru said: "Do not speak to me about him!
I venerate him rather as Death."
He who venerates him thus reaches a full lifespan in this world;
death does not come to him before his time.
Gārgya said: "The person who is here in the self—that very one I worship as Brahman.
Ajātaśatru said: "Do not talk to me about him! I worship him rather as 'the embodied one' (ātmanvī)."
He who venerates him thus becomes possessed of a self; his offspring become possessed of a self. Gārgya then remained silent.
Ajātaśatru said: "Is it only this much? "It is only this much," [Yājñavalkya replied].
"By this much alone, it is not known," [Ajātaśatru said].
Gārgya said: "Let me come to you as a pupil."
Ajātaśatru said: "It is contrary to the natural order that a Brāhmaṇa should approach a Kṣatriya thinking, 'He will tell me the Brahman.
Yet, I shall indeed make it known to you.
Taking him by the hand, he rose up.
The two of them came upon a man who was asleep.
They addressed him by these names: "Bṛhan! Pāṇḍaravāsa! Soma! Rājan!
But he did not rise.
He woke him by pressing him with his hand; he then rose up.
Ajātaśatru said: "When this person, who consists of consciousness, was thus asleep, where was he then? Whence did he come back? Gārgya did not know that.

Ajātaśatru said: "When this person consisting of consciousness was thus asleep—having taken to himself the consciousness of these vital breaths by means of his own consciousness—he lies in that space which is within the heart. When he takes hold of them..."
Now, when it is said that a person "sleeps," at that time the breath is indeed held,
and speech is held.
The eye is grasped;
the ear is grasped;
the mind is grasped. (Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad 2.1.17)
When he moves about in this state of dreaming, these indeed are his worlds;
then he becomes, as it were, a great king, or as it were, a great Brahmin, or he experiences various high and low conditions.

Just as a great king, having taken the subjects under his control, moves about in his own kingdom according to his pleasure, even so this [self], having taken hold of the vital breaths, moves about in its own body according to its pleasure.
Now, when one is fast asleep—
when one knows nothing at all—
there are seventy-two thousand channels called *hitā* that extend from the heart to the pericardium.
Having descended through them, he rests in the pericardium.
Just as a young boy, or a great king, or a great Brahmin might lie down after reaching the height of bliss, even so does he lie there. (Br̥hadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad 2.1.19)
Just as a spider moves along by means of its thread, or as tiny sparks fly forth from a fire, even so from this Self all vital breaths, all worlds, all deities,
and all beings emerge.
Its secret name (upaniṣad) is "the Truth of truth."
The vital breaths are indeed truth; he is their truth.
"Whoever knows the infant together with its support, its secondary support, its pillar, and its tether, holds back seven hateful rivals.
This very breath that is in the middle is indeed the infant;
this [lower body] is its support, this [upper body] is its secondary support, the breath is the pillar, and food is the tether. (Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad 2.2.1)
These seven abodes wait upon him.
Of these, those which are the red lines on the eye belong to Rudra;
and those which are the waters in the eye belong to Parjanya.
That which is the pupil is the Āditya;
that which is black is Agni;
that which is white is Indra.
The earth is dependent upon the lower course for its support;
the sky, upon the upper.
The food of one who knows this is never exhausted. (Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad 2.2.2)
Regarding this, there is this verse:
"A ladle with its opening below and its bottom above—in it is placed glory of every form.
Upon its bank sit the seven seers; speech is the eighth, attaining harmony with Brahman."

"The ladle is face-downward and upturned at the base. This refers to this very body, for it is indeed a ladle that is face-downward and upturned at the base. "In it glory is deposited, multiform"—this refers to the vital breaths (*prāṇāḥ*). For they are indeed glory, and they are multiform. "Therein all forms are contained"—this refers to the elements (*bhūtāni*), for therein all forms are indeed contained. "Thence arose the one-footed goat"—this refers to the year (*saṃvatsara*). For from the year alone did everything here arise. "The one-footed goat moves along"—this refers to the wind (*vāyu*). For the wind moves along as if on one foot. "The one-footed goat eats"—this refers to the sun (*āditya*). For the sun eats as if on one foot. "The one-footed goat sees"—this refers to the moon (*candramas*). For the moon sees as if on one foot. "The one-footed goat knows"—this refers to the mind (*manas*). For the mind knows as if on one foot. "The one-footed goat is the Brahman"—this refers to the *ātman*. For the *ātman* is indeed the Brahman. "The one-footed goat is the All"—this refers to the *ātman*. For the *ātman* is indeed the All. "The one-footed goat is the Truth"—this refers to the *ātman*. For the *ātman* is indeed the Truth. "The one-footed goat is the Infinite"—this refers to the *ātman*. "The one-footed goat is the Unrecoverable by name"—this refers to the *ātman*. For the *ātman* is indeed the Unrecoverable by name. "The one-footed goat is the Unrecoverable by earth"—this refers to the *ātman*. For the *ātman* is indeed the Unrecoverable by earth. "The one-footed goat is the Unrecoverable by water"—this refers to the *ātman*. For the *ātman* is indeed the Unrecoverable by water. "The one-footed goat is the Unrecoverable by fire"—this refers to the *ātman*. For the *ātman* is indeed the Unrecoverable by fire. "The one
The vital breaths are indeed glory, possessing all forms;
he thereby refers to the vital breaths.
"Of that which exists, there are seven seers on its bank."
The vital breaths are indeed the seers;
he says this regarding the vital breaths:
"Speech as the eighth, in harmony with the Brahman."
For speech, as the eighth, perceives through the Brahman.
These two are indeed Gotama and Bharadvāja;
this one is Gotama and this one is Bharadvāja.
These two are indeed Viśvāmitra and Jamadagni.
This is indeed Viśvāmitra; this is Jamadagni.
These two are Vasiṣṭha and Kaśyapa;
this is indeed Vasiṣṭha; this is Kaśyapa.
Speech indeed is Atri;
for by speech food is eaten. "Atri" is indeed the same as "eater" (attri).
He becomes the eater of all;
everything becomes his food—he who knows thus. (Br̥hadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad 2.2.4)
There are indeed two forms of Brahman:
the formed and the formless; the mortal and the immortal.
That which is stationary and that which moves;
that which exists and that which does not exist. Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad 2.3.1.
That which is other than air and the intermediate space is this embodied;
it is mortal;
it is stationary.
This is Being.
Of this embodied, mortal, stable, and existent Being, that which shines yonder is the essence;
for it is the essence of Being.
Now, that which is formless:
wind and the intermediate space;
this is the immortal.
This is that; this is Tyam.
Of this formless, immortal, and unshakable Tyam, the essence is this person who is in that orb.
For this is indeed its essence;
thus with respect to the divine. (Br̥hadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad 2.3.3)
Now, with reference to the self: that which is corporeal, other than the vital breath and this space within the self—
this is mortal.
This is that which is established; this is that which is real.
Of this embodied one, of this mortal one, of this established one, of this real one, the eye is the essence.
For this is the essence of the existent.
Now, that which is formless consists of the vital breath and this space within the self;
this is the immortal, this is the imperishable.
This is the "Tyat.
Of this formless, immortal, and moving "Tyat," that which is the person (puruṣa) in the right eye is the essence (rasa).
For he is indeed the essence of that "Tyat."
Now, the form of this very person is like a garment dyed with turmeric, like white wool, like a cochineal insect, like the flame of a fire, like a lotus, like a sudden flash of lightning. Indeed,
the splendor of one who knows this becomes like a sudden flash of lightning.
Now, therefore, follows the instruction: "Not this, not this.
For there is nothing else higher than this "not this.
Now, its name is "the Truth of truth."
The vital breaths (prāṇas) are indeed truth;
of them, this [Self] is the Truth.
"Maitreyī," Yājñavalkya said, "I am indeed about to depart from this place.
Come, let me make a final settlement between you and Kātyāyanī."

Maitreyī said: "But, O Venerable Sir, if this entire earth filled with wealth were mine, would I become immortal by means of it? "No," said Yājñavalkya, "your life would simply be like the life of those who possess such means."
"But there is no hope for immortality through wealth. (Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad 2.4.2)
Maitreyī said: "What should I do with that by which I would not become immortal?
Tell me only that which your reverence knows. (Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad 2.4.3)
Yājñavalkya said: "Truly, you are dear to us and you speak what is dear. Come, sit down;
I shall explain it to you."
"But while I am explaining it to you, reflect upon it. (Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad 2.4.4)

He said: "Verily, it is not out of love for the husband that the husband is dear, but it is out of love for the Self that the husband is dear. Verily, it is not out of love for the wife that the wife is dear, but it is out of love for the Self that the wife is dear.
Verily, it is not out of love for the sons that the sons are dear, but it is out of love for the Self that the sons are dear."

"Verily, it is not for the sake of wealth that wealth is dear; rather, it is for the sake of the Self that wealth is dear. Verily, it is not for the sake of the Brahminhood that the Brahminhood is dear; rather, it is for the sake of the Self that the Brahminhood is dear. Verily, it is not for the sake of the Kshatriyahood that the Kshatriyahood is dear; rather, it is for the sake of the Self that the Kshatriyahood is dear."
Verily, it is not for the sake of the worlds that the worlds are dear; rather, it is for the sake of the Self that the worlds are dear.

Verily, it is not for the sake of the gods that the gods are dear; rather, it is for the sake of the Self that the gods are dear. Verily, it is not for the sake of beings that beings are dear; rather, it is for the sake of the Self that beings are dear.
"Verily, it is not for the sake of all that all becomes dear; rather, it is for the sake of the Self that all becomes dear.
Verily, the Self, O Maitreyī, should be seen, heard, reflected upon, and meditated upon.
Verily, by seeing, hearing, reflecting upon, and realizing the Self, all this is known. (Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad 2.4.5)
Brahman deserts him who knows Brahman as other than the Self; Kshatra deserts him who knows Kshatra as other than the Self;
the worlds desert him who knows the worlds as other than the Self.
The gods desert him who knows the gods as other than the Self;
the beings desert him who knows the beings as other than the Self;
everything deserts him who knows everything as other than the Self.
This is Brahman, this is Kṣatra, these are the worlds, these are the gods, these are all beings—this entire world is that which is this Self.
Just as, when a drum is being beaten, one cannot grasp the external sounds;
but by grasping the drum, or the striking of the drum, the sound is grasped. (Br̥hadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad 2.4.7)

Just as when a conch shell is being blown, one would not be able to grasp the external sounds; rather, by grasping the conch shell or the blower of the conch, the sound is grasped. Just as when a lute is being played, one would not be able to grasp the external sounds; rather, by grasping the lute or the player of the lute, the sound is grasped.

Just as from a fire of damp wood, when kindled, various clouds of smoke issue forth, even so, my dear, this Rigveda, Yajurveda, Samaveda, Atharvangirasa, history, ancient lore, sciences, Upanishads, verses, aphorisms, explanations, and commentaries are the breath of this great Being.
These are indeed his very breaths.
Just as the ocean is the single point of convergence for all waters,
so the skin is the single point of convergence for all tactile sensations; so the two nostrils are the single point of convergence for all odors.
In this way, the tongue is the single point of convergence for all tastes; in this way, the eye is the single point of convergence for all forms;
in this way, the ear is the single point of convergence for all sounds.
In this way, the mind is the single point of convergence for all volitions;
in this way, the heart is the single point of convergence for all branches of knowledge;
in this way, the two hands are the single point of convergence for all actions.
In this way, the organ of generation is the single point of convergence for all forms of pleasure;
in this way, the anus is the single point of convergence for all excretions;
in this way, the feet are the single point of convergence for all paths.
In this way, speech is the single point of convergence for all the Vedas.

Just as a lump of salt, when thrown into water, dissolves completely into the water so that it cannot be taken up again, yet from whichever part one takes, it is salty— just so, my dear, this great being is infinite, boundless, and a mass of pure consciousness alone.
"Arising from these very elements, one perishes after them.
There is no consciousness after death," thus, O venerable one, Yājñavalkya said. *Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad* 2.4.12.

Maitreyī said: "Right here, my lord, you have bewildered me by saying that there is no consciousness after death. He replied: "Indeed, I do not speak a bewildering thing, O dear one; this is sufficient for understanding. *Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad* 2.4.13.

For where there is duality, as it were, there one smells another; there one sees another; there one hears another; there one smells another; there one speaks to another; there one thinks of another; there one understands another.
But when for him everything has become the Self alone, then by what and whom should he smell? Then by what and whom should he smell?

Then by what and whom should he see? Then by what and whom should he hear? Then by what and whom should he speak? Then by what and whom should he think? Then by what and whom should he know? By what should he know that by which one knows all this?
"By what means, my dear, could one know the knower? (Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad 2.4.14)
This earth is honey for all beings;
all beings are honey for this earth.
That radiant, immortal person who is in this earth, and that radiant, immortal person who is in the body with respect to the self—this very one is the Self.
This is the immortal, this is Brahman, this is all.
These waters are honey for all beings;
all beings are honey for these waters.

And this person within these waters, consisting of splendor and consisting of immortality, and this person within the self consisting of semen, consisting of splendor and consisting of immortality—he is indeed this Self.
This is the immortal, this is Brahman, this is all.
This fire is honey for all beings;
all beings are honey for this fire.

And that person consisting of splendor and consisting of immortality who is in this fire, and that person consisting of speech, consisting of splendor, and consisting of immortality who is with respect to the self (adhyātma)—this very one is the Self (ātman).
This is the immortal, this is Brahman, this is all.
This wind is honey for all beings;
all beings are honey for this wind.

And that person who is in this wind, consisting of light and consisting of immortality, and that person who is here in the self (adhyātma), the vital breath (prāṇa), consisting of light and consisting of immortality—he is indeed this Self.
This is the immortal, this is Brahman, this is all.
This Āditya is honey for all beings;
all beings are honey for this Āditya.

And that person who is here in this Āditya, consisting of splendor and consisting of immortality, and that person who is here in the self (adhyātma) as the ocular one, consisting of splendor and consisting of immortality—he is indeed this very Self.
This is the immortal, this is Brahman, this is all.
These quarters are honey for all beings;
all beings are honey for these quarters.

And that person consisting of splendor and consisting of immortality who is in these quarters, and that person consisting of splendor and consisting of immortality who is within the self—the one connected with hearing and the one connected with the echo—he is indeed this very Self.
This is the immortal; this is Brahman; this is all.
This moon is honey for all beings;
all beings are honey for this moon.

And that person consisting of splendor, consisting of nectar, who is in this moon, and that person consisting of splendor, consisting of nectar, who is in the self with respect to the mind—he is indeed this very Self, this nectar.
This Brahman is all this.
This lightning is honey for all beings;
all beings are honey for this lightning.

And that person who is within this lightning, consisting of splendor, consisting of immortality, and that person who is within the self (adhyātma), consisting of splendor, consisting of splendor, consisting of immortality—he is indeed this Self.
This is the immortal, this is Brahman, this is all.
This thunder is honey for all beings;
all beings are honey for this thunder.

And that person consisting of splendor and consisting of immortality who is in this thunder, and that person consisting of splendor and consisting of immortality who is the one relating to sound (*śābda*) within the self (*adhyātma*), the one belonging to the Svara—he is indeed this very Self.
This is the immortal, this is Brahman, this is all.
This space is honey for all beings;
all beings are honey for this space.

And that person who is here in this space, consisting of light and consisting of immortality, and that person who is here within the self (adhyātma) in the space of the heart, consisting of light and consisting of immortality—he is indeed this very Self.
This is the immortal, this is Brahman, this is all.
This Dharma is honey for all beings;
all beings are honey for this Dharma.
And that radiant, immortal person who is in this Dharma, and that radiant, immortal person who is the internal self (adhyātma) consisting of Dharma—this is indeed that which is the Self (ātman).
This is the immortal, this is Brahman, this is all.
This truth is honey for all beings;
all beings are honey for this truth.
And that radiant, immortal person who is in this truth, and that radiant, immortal person who is the self within the body consisting of truth—this very one is the Self.
This is the immortal, this is Brahman, this is all.
This human being is honey for all beings;
all beings are honey for this human being.

And that person consisting of splendor, consisting of immortality, who is in this human being, and that person consisting of splendor, consisting of immortality, who is the human self within the body—this very one is the Self (Ātman).
This is the immortal, this is Brahman, this is all.
This self is honey for all beings;
all beings are honey for this self.
And that person consisting of splendor and consisting of immortality who is in this self, and this self consisting of splendor and consisting of immortality—that is indeed this very self.
This is the immortal, this is Brahman, this is all.

This Self, indeed, is the overlord of all, the king of all beings. Just as all the spokes are fixed in the nave and the felly of a chariot wheel, even so in this Self all beings, all gods, all worlds, all vital breaths, and all these selves are fixed. (Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad 2.5.15)
This indeed is that honey which Dadhyañc Ātharvaṇa spoke to the two Aśvins.

Seeing this, the seer declared: "O Heroes, I make manifest for you that powerful deed for the sake of gain, as thunder makes rain manifest—that honey which Dadhyañc Ātharvaṇa spoke to you by means of the horse's head."
This indeed is that honey which Dadhyañc Ātharvaṇa spoke to the two Aśvins.

Seeing this, the seer declared: "O Aśvins, you restored the horse's head to Dadhyañc Ātharvaṇa; he, abiding by the Truth, proclaimed the honey to you—the Tvaṣṭṛ-made [knowledge] which was hidden in your secret place, O wonder-workers. (Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad 2.5.17)
This indeed is that honey which Dadhyañc Ātharvaṇa spoke to the Aśvins.
Seeing this, a seer declared: "He made bodies with two feet; he made bodies with four feet.
Having first become a bird, he entered the bodies as the Puruṣa."
Verily, this person dwells within all cities;
there is nothing by which he is not covered,
and there is nothing by which he is not enclosed.

This indeed is that honey which Dadhyañc Ātharvaṇa spoke to the Aśvins. Seeing this, the seer declared: "In form after form he became a counterpart; that is his form for the sake of being perceived. Indra moves in many forms through his powers of illusion (māyā), for his bay horses are yoked, a hundred and ten."
This indeed is the golden one; this indeed is the ten, the thousands, the many, and the infinite.
This very Brahman is without before, without after, without within, and without without.
This Self is Brahman, the experiencer of all.
Thus is the instruction. BrhUp 2.5.19.

Brahman is self-existent.
Homage to Brahman. BrhUp 2.6.3.
Janaka of Videha performed a sacrifice at which many gifts were distributed.
There, the Brahmins of the Kurus and Pañcālas had gathered together.
Janaka of Videha desired to know: "Who among these Brahmins is the most learned in the Vedas?"
He enclosed a thousand cows;
ten pādas were tied to the horns of each individual cow.
He said to them: "Venerable Brahmins, let him among you who is most proficient in Brahman drive away these cows.
Those Brahmins did not dare.
Then Yājñavalkya said to his own pupil: "Sāmaśrava, my dear, drive these away."
He did so; those Brahmins were enraged, saying:
"How can he who is the most learned in the Veda speak to us thus?"
Now, Āśvala was the Hotṛ priest of Janaka of Videha.
He questioned him: "Yājñavalkya, are you indeed the most proficient in Brahman among us?
He replied: "We pay homage to the one most proficient in Brahman; we are merely seekers of cattle."
Then the Hotṛ Āśvala resolved to question him right there.
"Yājñavalkya," he said, "since all this is overtaken by death, since all is seized by death, by what means does the sacrificer transcend the reach of death?
"By the Hotṛ priest, by the fire, and by speech.
"For speech, indeed, is the Hotṛ of the sacrifice."
Now, this speech is this very fire; it is the Hotṛ priest; it is liberation; it is complete liberation.
"Yājñavalkya," he said, "since all this is pervaded by day and night, and all is encompassed by day and night, by what means does the sacrificer transcend the pervasion of day and night?
"By the Adhvaryu priest, who is the eye, and by Āditya.
"The eye, indeed, is the Adhvaryu of the sacrifice."
Therefore, this eye is that very sun;
it is the Adhvaryu priest; it is liberation; it is complete liberation.

"Yājñavalkya," he said, "since all this is pervaded by the first and second fortnights, and all is encompassed by the first and second fortnights, by what means does the sacrificer transcend the pervasion of the first and second fortnights? "By the Udgātṛ priest, by wisdom, and by the vital breath."
The Udgātṛ of the sacrifice is indeed the vital breath (prāṇa).
Now, that which is this vital breath is Vāyu; he is the Udgātṛ. He is liberation; he is complete liberation.
"Yājñavalkya," he said, "by what means does the sacrificer ascend to the heavenly world from this atmosphere which is, as it were, without support?
By the Brahman priest, by the mind, by the moon.
For the mind is indeed the Brahman of the sacrifice."
Thus, this mind is that moon; it is Brahmā, it is liberation, it is perfect liberation—these are the "deliverances. Now, the "attainments. Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad 3.1.6.

"With three," [Yājñavalkya replied].
"Which are those three?"
