"O Yājñavalkya," he said, "how many oblations will this Adhvaryu priest offer today in this sacrifice?
"Three. "Which are those three?"
"What does one win by those oblations which blaze up when offered, those which overflow when offered, and those which lie still when offered?
"One wins the world of the gods by those oblations which blaze up when offered."
For the world of the gods seems as if ablaze;
those [oblations] which pass beyond reach conquer the world of the fathers,
for the world of the fathers is exceedingly vast.
Those oblations which lie upon the fire-altar, by means of them he conquers the world of men;
for the world of men is, as it were, below.
"O Yājñavalkya," he said, "with how many deities does this Brahman protect the sacrifice from the south today?
"With one. "Which is that one?"
"It is mind alone.
Mind is indeed infinite, and the All-Gods are infinite.
By means of that [mind], he conquers an infinite world.
"Yājñavalkya," he said, "how many *stotriyas* will this Udgātṛ chant today in this sacrifice? "Three," [he replied].
"Which are those three?"
The invitatory verse (*puronuvākyā*), the offering verse (*yājyā*), and the recitation (*śasyā*) as the third—
what are these? Those which are "with reference to the self" (*adhyātma*).
The *prāṇa* (out-breath) is the *puronuvākyā*, the *apāna* (in-breath) is the *yājyā*, and the *vyāna* (diffused breath) is the *śasyā*.
What does one win by means of these?
One wins the world of earth by the *puronuvākyā*, the world of the intermediate space by the *yājyā*, and the world of heaven by the *śasyā*.
Thereupon, Aśvala the Hotṛ ceased questioning.
Then Ārtabhāga Jāratkārava questioned him.
"Yājñavalkya," he said, "how many are the *grahas* (seizers) and how many are the *atigrahas* (over-seizers)?
"There are eight *grahas* and eight *atigrahas*."
"Those eight graspers and eight over-graspers—what are they? (Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad 3.2.1)
The out-breath (prāṇa) is indeed the grasper; it is seized by the out-breath as the over-grasper,
for by means of the out-breath one smells odors.
Speech, indeed, is a grasper;
it is seized by the name as its over-grasper,
for by means of speech one utters names.
The tongue, indeed, is a grasper;
it is seized by taste as the over-grasper, for by means of the tongue one perceives tastes. (Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad 3.2.4)
The eye, indeed, is a grasper;
it is seized by form as the over-grasper,
for by means of the eye one sees forms.
The ear, indeed, is a grasper;
it is seized by sound as its over-grasper,
for by means of the ear one hears sounds.
The mind, indeed, is a grasper; it is seized by desire as the over-grasper,
for by means of the mind one desires desires.
The hands, indeed, are the grasper;
they are seized by action as the over-grasper,
for it is with the hands that one performs action.
The skin, indeed, is the grasper;
it is seized by touch as the over-grasper,
for by means of the skin one perceives touches.
Thus there are eight graspers and eight over-graspers.
"Yājñavalkya," he said, "since all this is food for death, who is that deity for whom death is food?
"Fire, indeed, is death; it is the food of water. [By knowing this] one conquers recurrent death. (Br̥hadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad 3.2.10)
"O Yājñavalkya," he said, "when this person dies, do his vital breaths depart from him, or do they not? "No," said Yājñavalkya,
"they are simply absorbed right here."
It swells up;
it becomes bloated;
bloated, it lies dead.
"O Yājñavalkya," he said, "when this person dies, what does not leave him?
"His name," [he replied].
"Ananta" indeed is its name; the All-gods (Viśvedevas) are infinite.
Through that [name], he conquers an infinite world.

"O Yājñavalkya," he said, "when the speech of this dead person enters into fire, his breath into the wind, his sight into the sun, his mind into the moon, his hearing into the quarters, his body into the earth, his self (ātman) into space, the hairs of his body into herbs, the hairs of his head into trees, and his blood and semen are deposited in the waters— then where does this person become?"
"Come, gentle Ārtabhāga, let us two alone understand this; let it not be common knowledge between us.
Having stepped aside, the two of them conferred.
What those two said was indeed action;
what they praised was indeed action. "One becomes virtuous by virtuous action and evil by evil action."
Thereupon, Ārtabhāga, the son of Jaratkāru, ceased questioning.
Then Bhujyu Lāhyāyani questioned him. "Yājñavalkya," he said, "we were traveling among the Madras as wandering students.
We came to the house of Patañcala Kāpya.
He had a daughter who was possessed by a Gandharva."
We asked him, "Who are you?
He replied, "I am Sudhanvan Āṅgirasa. When we asked him about the ends of the worlds, he said:
Then we said to him: "Where did the Pārikṣitas go?
Where did the Pārikṣitas go? That is what I ask you, Yājñavalkya."
"Where did the sons of Parikṣit go? Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad 3.3.1.
He said: "He indeed spoke thus:
'They surely went to that place where those who perform the Aśvamedha sacrifice go.
[The other asked: 'Where, pray, do those who perform the Aśvamedha sacrifice go?'"
This world extends for thirty-two days' journey by a divine chariot; the earth encircles it on all sides with twice that distance,
and the ocean encircles the earth on all sides with twice that distance.
As much as the edge of a razor or the wing of a fly—just so great was the space between them. Indra, having become a *suparṇa* bird, delivered them to Vāyu.
Vāyu, having placed them within himself, brought them to that place where the performers of the horse sacrifice had been.
In this very way, he indeed praised Vāyu alone; therefore, Vāyu is the individual manifestation (*vyaṣṭi*) and Vāyu is the collective manifestation (*samaṣṭi*).
"He who knows this overcomes repeated death. Thereupon, Bhujyu Lāhyāyani ceased questioning.
Then Uṣasta Cākrāyaṇa questioned him.
"O Yājñavalkya," he said, "explain to me that Brahman which is immediate and direct, that Self which is within all.
"This is your Self, which is within all."

He who breathes in with the in-breath (prāṇa) is your Self, dwelling within all; he who breathes out with the out-breath (apāna) is your Self, dwelling within all; he who breathes through with the diffused breath (vyāna) is your Self, dwelling within all.
That which breathes out with the out-breath—that is your self, the innermost of all;
this is your self, the innermost of all.
Uṣasta Cākrāyaṇa said: "Just as one might say, 'This is a cow' or 'This is a horse,' so indeed has this been designated.
Please explain to me that Brahman which is manifest and not hidden, the Self that is within all. [The teacher replied:
"This is your Self, which is within all."
"Which one, Yājñavalkya, is the innermost of all?
"You would not see the seer of seeing;
you would not hear the hearer of hearing."
Do not think of the thinker of thought; do not seek to know the knower of knowledge.
This is your Self, which is within all.
"Anything other than this is afflicted.
Thereupon, Uṣasta Cākrāyaṇa ceased questioning.
Then Kahola Kauṣītakeya questioned him: "O Yājñavalkya," he said, "explain to me that Brahman which is immediate and direct, that Self which is within all.
"This is your Self, which is within all."
"Who, Yājñavalkya, is the innermost of all?
He who transcends hunger and thirst, sorrow and delusion, old age and death.
Having known this very Self, the Brahmins rise above the desire for sons, the desire for wealth, and the desire for worlds, and then lead the life of mendicants."
For that which is the desire for sons is the desire for wealth, and that which is the desire for wealth is the desire for worlds;
indeed, both of these are simply desires.
Therefore, a Brahmin, having become disillusioned with scholarship, should seek to abide in childlike innocence.
Having become disillusioned with both childhood and scholarship, one is then a sage;
having become disillusioned with both non-silence and silence, one is then a brahmin.
By what would he be a brahmin? He is exactly such as he is by that very state.
"Anything other than this is afflicted.
Thereupon, Kahola Kauṣītakeya ceased questioning.

Then Gārgī Vācaknavī questioned him. "Yājñavalkya," she said, "this entire world is woven like warp and woof upon the waters; upon what, then, are the waters woven like warp and woof? "Upon the wind, Gārgī."
"In what, then, is the wind woven to and fro? "In the worlds of the intermediate space, Gārgī. "In what, then, are the worlds of the intermediate space woven to and fro?"
“In the worlds of the Gandharvas, Gārgī.
“But in what, indeed, are the worlds of the Gandharvas woven to and fro?
“In the worlds of Āditya, Gārgī.”
"But in what, indeed, are the worlds of the sun woven back and forth?
"In the worlds of the moon, Gārgī.
"But in what, indeed, are the worlds of the moon woven back and forth?"
"In the worlds of the stars, Gārgī," he said.
"In what, then, are the worlds of the stars woven to and fro?
"In the worlds of the gods, Gārgī."
"In what, indeed, are the worlds of the gods woven to and fro?
"In the worlds of Indra, Gārgī.
"In what, indeed, are the worlds of Indra woven to and fro?"
"In the worlds of Prajāpati, Gārgī.
"But in what, indeed, are the worlds of Prajāpati woven to and fro?
"In the worlds of Brahman, Gārgī."
"In what, indeed, are the worlds of Brahmā woven to and fro?
He said, "Gārgī, do not ask beyond this, lest your head shatter apart."
"You are indeed asking too much of a deity that should not be questioned beyond this. Gārgī, do not ask too much! Thereupon, Gārgī Vācaknavī ceased questioning.
Then Uddālaka Āruṇi questioned him. "Yājñavalkya," he said, "we were staying among the Madras in the house of Patañcala Kāpya, studying the sacrifice.
His wife was possessed by a Gandharva."
We asked him, "Who are you?
He replied, "I am Kabandha Ātharvaṇa.
He then said to Patañcala Kāpya and the ritualists, "Do you know, O Kāpya, that thread by which this world, the other world, and all beings are strung together?"
"They exist," [the other said].
Patañcala Kāpya replied, "I do not know that, O Blessed One.
He then spoke to Patañcala Kāpya and the ritualists.
"Do you know, O Kāpya, that inner controller who controls from within this world and the next world, and all beings?
Patañcala Kāpya replied, "I do not know him, O Blessed One.
He then spoke to Patañcala Kāpya and the ritualists.

"O Kāpya, whoever indeed knows that thread and him who is the inner controller—he is a knower of Brahman, he is a knower of the worlds, he is a knower of the gods, he is a knower of the Vedas, he is a knower of the Self, he is a knower of all.
Thus he spoke to them.
That I know.

"If you, Yājñavalkya, being ignorant of that thread and that inner controller, drive away the cows of Brahman, your head shall fall off. "I do indeed know that thread and that inner controller, O Gautama. "Whoever might say here, 'I know, I know,' tell us how you know it. (Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad 3.7.1)
He said: "O Gautama, that thread is indeed wind.
By the thread of wind, O Gautama, this world, the other world, and all beings are held together.
Therefore, O Gautama, they say of a dead man: 'His limbs have fallen apart.'"

"For they are strung together by the thread of wind, Gautama. "Just so, Yājñavalkya. Speak of the inner controller. ||| BrhUp_3,7.2 ||| "By the thread of wind, Gautama, they are indeed strung together.
"It is even so, Yājñavalkya. Speak of the inner controller," [he said]. ||| BrhUp_3,7.2 |||
He who dwells in the earth, yet is within the earth, whom the earth does not know, whose body is the earth, who controls the earth from within—He is your Self, the Inner Controller, the Immortal.
He who dwells in the waters, yet is within the waters, whom the waters do not know, whose body is the waters, who controls the waters from within—he is your Self, the Inner Controller, the Immortal.
He who, dwelling in fire, is within fire, whom fire does not know, whose body is fire, who controls fire from within—he is your Self, the inner controller, the immortal.

He who, dwelling in the intermediate space, is within the intermediate space, whom the intermediate space does not know, whose body is the intermediate space, who controls the intermediate space from within—He is your Self, the Inner Controller, the Immortal.
He who, dwelling in the wind, is within the wind, whom the wind does not know, whose body is the wind, who controls the wind from within—He is your Self, the Inner Controller, the Immortal.
He who dwells in heaven, yet is within heaven, whom heaven does not know, whose body is heaven, who controls heaven from within—He is your Self, the Inner Controller, the Immortal.

He who, dwelling in the sun, is within the sun, whom the sun does not know, whose body is the sun, who controls the sun from within—he is your Self, the Inner Controller, the Immortal. He who, dwelling in the quarters, is within the quarters, whom the quarters do not know, whose body is the quarters, who controls the quarters from within—he is your Self, the Inner Controller, the Immortal.

He who dwells in the moon and the stars, yet is within the moon and the stars, whom the moon and the stars do not know, whose body is the moon and the stars, who controls the moon and the stars from within—
He is your Self, the Inner Controller, the Immortal.

He who dwells in space, yet is within space, whom space does not know, whose body is space, who controls space from within—He is your Self, the Inner Controller, the Immortal. (Br̥hadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad 3.7.12)

He who dwells in darkness, yet is within darkness, whom darkness does not know, whose body is darkness, who controls darkness from within—He is your Self, the Inner Controller, the Immortal. He who dwells in light, yet is within light, whom light does not know, whose body is light, who controls light from within—He is your Self, the Inner Controller, the Immortal.
Now, with respect to the elements (adhibhūta):

"He who, dwelling within all beings, is distinct from all beings; whom all beings do not know; whose body all beings are; who controls all beings from within—he is your Self, the Inner Controller, the Immortal. Thus far with respect to the elemental realm (*adhibhūta*). *Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad* 3.7.15.
Now, with reference to the self:

He who dwells in the vital breath (*prāṇa*), yet is within the vital breath; whom the vital breath does not know; whose body is the vital breath; who controls the vital breath from within—He is your Self, the Inner Controller, the Immortal. He who dwells in speech (*vāc*), yet is within speech; whom speech does not know; whose body is speech; who controls speech from within—He is your Self, the Inner Controller, the Immortal.

He who dwells in the eye, yet is within the eye, whom the eye does not know, whose body is the eye, who controls the eye from within—He is your Self, the Inner Controller, the Immortal. He who dwells in the ear, yet is within the ear, whom the ear does not know, whose body is the ear, who controls the ear from within—He is your Self, the Inner Controller, the Immortal.
He who, dwelling in the mind, is within the mind, whom the mind does not know, whose body is the mind, who controls the mind from within—He is your Self, the Inner Controller, the Immortal.
He who, dwelling in the skin, is within the skin, whom the skin does not know, whose body is the skin, who controls the skin from within—he is your Self, the inner controller, the immortal.

He who, dwelling in consciousness, is within consciousness, whom consciousness does not know, whose body is consciousness, who controls consciousness from within—He is your Self, the Inner Controller, the Immortal. He who, dwelling in semen, is within semen, whom semen does not know, whose body is semen, who controls semen from within—He is your Self, the Inner Controller, the Immortal.
Unseen, yet the Seer; unheard, yet the Hearer; unthought, yet the Thinker; unknown, yet the Knower.
Other than this, there is no seer; other than this, there is no hearer; other than this, there is no thinker; other than this, there is no knower.
This is your Self, the inner controller, the immortal.
Other than this, everything is subject to suffering.
Thereupon, Uddālaka Āruṇi desisted.
Then Vācaknavī said: "Venerable Brahmins, come now, I shall ask him two questions. If he can answer them for me, then indeed none of you will ever defeat him in this debate on Brahman."
"Ask, Gārgī," he said.

She said: "O Yājñavalkya, just as a warrior-son of the Kāśis or the Videhas might rise up, having strung a bow with an unstrung string and taking in his hands two arrows capable of piercing through adversaries, even so have I risen up against you with two questions."
"Tell them both to me," [he said].
"Ask, Gārgī," [he replied]. (Br̥hadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad 3.8.2)

She said: "Yājñavalkya, that which is above the sky, that which is below the earth, that which is between these two, heaven and earth, and that which they call the past, the present, and the future—in what are all these woven to and fro?"

He said: "O Gārgī, that which is above the sky, that which is below the earth, that which is between these two, heaven and earth, and that which they call the past, the present, and the future—across all this, [the Imperishable] is woven as the warp and the woof."
She said, "Homage be to you, Yājñavalkya, who has explained this to me; hold fast for another [question]. "Ask, Gārgī," he said.

She said: "Yājñavalkya, that which is above the sky, that which is below the earth, that which is between these two—the heaven and the earth—and that which they call the past, the present, and the future—across what is that woven, warp and woof?"

He said: "That which is above the sky, Gārgī, that which is below the earth, that which is between these two, heaven and earth, and that which they call the past, the present, and the future—all that is woven, warp and woof, upon space alone. "But upon what, then, is space woven, warp and woof? (Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad 3.8.7)
He said: "O Gārgī, the Brahmins indeed describe that Imperishable as neither gross nor subtle,

neither short nor long, neither red nor oily, neither shadowy nor dark, neither air nor space, without attachment, without taste, without smell, without eyes, without ears, without speech, without mind, without radiance, without breath, without mouth, without body, without interior and without exterior."
Nothing whatsoever eats that;
no one whatsoever eats that.
"By the command of this Imperishable, O Gārgī, the sun and the moon stand held apart;
by the command of this Imperishable, O Gārgī, heaven and earth stand held apart;
by the command of this Imperishable, O Gārgī, the moments, the hours, the days and nights, the half-months, the months, the seasons, and the years stand held apart."
"Under the governance of this very Imperishable, O Gārgī, some rivers flow eastward from the white mountains, and others flow toward every other direction.
Under the governance of this very Imperishable, O Gārgī, humans praise the sacrificer; the gods depend upon the oblation-ladle, and the ancestors depend upon the ancestral offering."

Or, O Gārgī, whoever in this world offers oblations, performs sacrifices, or practices austerities for many thousands of years without knowing this Imperishable— one whose [merit] comes to an end; and whoever departs from this world, O Gārgī, without knowing this Imperishable, he is pitiable.
Now, Gārgī, he who departs from this world after having known this imperishable syllable—he is a true Brahmin.
Now, this very syllable, O Gārgī, is the unseen seer, the unheard hearer, the unthought thinker, the unknown knower.
There is no other seer than this;
there is no other hearer than this.
There is no other thinker than this;
there is no other knower than this.
Indeed, O Gārgī, in this very Imperishable, space is woven like warp and woof.
She said: "Venerable Brahmins, you should consider yourselves fortunate enough if you can escape from us merely by paying homage.
Indeed, no one will ever defeat you in this debate on Brahman.
Thereupon, Gārgī Vācaknavī ceased questioning.

Then Vidagdha Śākalya questioned him: "How many gods are there, Yājñavalkya? He answered with this very *nivid*: as many as are mentioned in the *nivid* of the Vaiśvadeva hymn—"Three hundred and three, and three thousand and three."
"Om," he said. "How many gods are there, Yājñavalkya?
"Thirty-three," he replied.
"Om," he said. "How many gods are there, Yājñavalkya? "Six," he replied.
"Om," he said. "How many gods are there, Yājñavalkya? "Three," he replied.
"Om," he said. "How many gods are there, Yājñavalkya? "Two."
"Om," he said. "How many gods are there, Yājñavalkya? "One and a half," he replied.
"Om," he said. "How many gods are there, Yājñavalkya? "One," he replied.
"Om," he said.
"Which are those three and three hundred, and three and three thousand? 3.9.1.
He said: "These are merely their manifestations;
there are, however, only thirty-three gods.
"Which are those thirty-three? he asked.
There are eight Vasus, eleven Rudras, and twelve Ādityas; these make thirty-one, and with Indra and Prajāpati, they are thirty-three.
"Who are the Vasus? "Fire, earth, wind, the intermediate space, the sun, the sky, the moon, and the stars—these are the Vasus.
For in these all this wealth (*vasu*) is contained; therefore they are called the Vasus. (Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad 3.9.3)
"What are the Rudras?
"These ten vital breaths in a person, with the self as the eleventh;
when they depart from this mortal body, then they cause one to weep."
Because they cause weeping, therefore they are called Rudras.
"What are the Ādityas? "The twelve months of the year are indeed these Ādityas;
for they go along taking up everything here."
Because they go taking all this [wealth] with them, they are called Ādityas.
"What is Indra? What is Prajāpati? "The thunderclap is indeed Indra; the sacrifice is Prajāpati.
"What is the thunderclap?"
"Lightning," he said.
"What is the sacrifice? "Animals," he replied. (Br̥hadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad 3.9.6)
"What are the six?
"Fire, earth, wind, the intermediate space, the sun, and the sky—these are the six.
For these indeed are all this [universe] as the six. (Br̥hadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad 3.9.7)
"What are those three gods? [He replied: "These very three worlds; for within these, all these gods are contained."
"Which are those two deities? "Food and breath.
"Which is the one-and-a-half?"
"This is that which blows. (Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad 3.9.8)

Regarding this they say: "Since this [wind] blows as if it were one alone, how then is it 'one and a half' (adhyardha)? Because everything here has grown beyond (adhyārdhnot) within it, therefore it is called "one and a half."
"What is that one deity?
"The vital breath (prāṇa). "That is Brahman; they call it 'That' (tyad). Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad 3.9.9.

"He who knows that person whose abode is the earth itself, whose world is fire, whose light is the mind, and who is the ultimate resort of every self—he indeed would be a knower. "Yājñavalkya, I do know that person, the ultimate resort of every self, of whom you speak.
He is this very person consisting of the body."
"Tell me, Śākalya, who is the deity of that? "Immortality," he replied.

"He for whom desire is the abode, the heart is the world, and the mind is the light—verily, he who would know that person, the ultimate resort of every self, he indeed would be a knower. "Yājñavalkya, I do indeed know that person, the ultimate resort of every self, of whom you speak.
That very person consisting of desire is this one here."
"Tell me, Śākalya, who is its deity? "Women," he replied.

"He for whom visible forms alone are the sphere, whose world is the eye, and whose light is the mind—he who indeed knows that person, the ultimate resort of every self, he would truly be a knower. "Yājñavalkya, I do indeed know that person, the ultimate resort of every self, of whom you speak.
That very person who is there in the sun, he is this one."
"Tell me, Śākalya, who is its deity?
"Truth," he replied. (Br̥hadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad 3.9.12)
"He for whom space alone is the abode, whose world is the ear, and whose light is the mind—he who would know that person, the ultimate resort of every self, he indeed would be a knower.
"Yājñavalkya, I do indeed know that person, the ultimate resort of every self, of whom you speak.
That very person who is heard and who is perceived through hearing—that is he."
"Tell me, Śākalya, who is its deity? "The quarters," he replied.

"He whose abode is darkness, whose world is the heart, and whose light is the mind—verily, he who knows that person, the ultimate resort of every self, would indeed be a knower. "Yājñavalkya, do I not know that person, the ultimate resort of every self, of whom you speak? It is this very person consisting of shadow. "No, that is not he, O Śākalya; for you have described him merely as one who possesses knowledge of the deities, and you shall become one of those whose head will fall off. "If you say so, Yājñavalkya, then my head will surely fall off," said Śākalya. "Let it fall, if you like," said Yājñavalkya. And his head fell off. Their food is the red lump in the heart. Their covering is the net-like membrane in the heart. The path leading away from them is the channel that extends from the heart upward to the throat; when one is about to depart, one sees this channel as a white light. "Tell me, Śākalya, who is the deity of that? "Death," he replied. *Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad* 3.9.14.

"He for whom visible forms alone are the sphere, the heart, the world, and the light of the mind—he who would know that person, the ultimate resort of every self, he indeed would be a knower. "Yājñavalkya, I do indeed know that person, the ultimate resort of every self, of whom you speak.
That very person who is here in the mirror is he."
"Tell me, Śākalya, who is its deity?
"Truth," he replied. (Br̥hadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad 3.9.15)

"He for whom water is the abode, the heart is the world, and the mind is the light—that person, indeed, one who should know him as the ultimate resort of every self, would truly be a knower. "Yājñavalkya, I do indeed know that person, the ultimate resort of every self, of whom you speak.
That very person who is here in the waters, he is this one."
"Tell me, Śākalya, who is its deity?
"Varuṇa," he said.
"He whose abode is semen, whose world is the heart, and whose light is the mind—he who would know that person, the ultimate resort of every self, he indeed would be a knower.
"Yājñavalkya, do I not know that person, the ultimate resort of every self, of whom you speak?
That very person consisting of a son is this one here."
"Tell me, Śākalya, who is its deity? "Prajāpati," he replied. *Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad* 3.9.17.
"Śākalya," said Yājñavalkya,
"have these Brahmins indeed made you their charcoal-pit?"
"Yājñavalkya," said Śākalya,
"since you have outtalked the Brahmins of the Kurus and Pañcālas, what do you know as Brahman?
"I know the quarters together with their deities and their foundations."
The quarters of space you know, together with the gods and their foundations.
"Which deity are you in this eastern direction?
"The sun is my deity.
"In what is that sun established?"
"Regarding the eyes:
upon what, then, is the eye established? "Upon visible forms."
"For one sees forms with the eye. But in what, then, are forms established?
"In the heart," he said.
"For by means of the heart one knows forms;
for in the heart alone forms are established.
"It is even so, Yājñavalkya. *Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad* 3.9.20.
"Which deity are you in this southern direction?
"Yama is my deity. "In what is that Yama established?"
"Regarding sacrifice:
on what, indeed, is sacrifice established?
"On the sacrificial fee."
"On what, then, is the sacrificial gift (dakṣiṇā) established? "On faith (śraddhā)," he replied. "For it is only when one has faith that one gives the sacrificial gift."
"For the sacrificial gift is established upon faith alone.
"But upon what is faith established?
"Upon the heart," he said.
"For faith [is established] by means of the heart; for faith is indeed established in the heart. "It is just so, Yājñavalkya. *Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad* 3.9.21.
"Which deity presides over you in this western direction?
"Varuṇa is my deity.
"In what is that Varuṇa established?"
"In the waters. "In what, then, are the waters established? "In semen."

"In what, then, is semen established? "In the heart. Therefore, even when a person who resembles [the father] is born, they say of him: "He has slipped as if from the heart; he has been fashioned as if from the heart."
"For semen is indeed established in the heart," [said Maitreyī].
"It is just so, Yājñavalkya."
"Which deity presides over this northern direction?
"Soma is its deity.
"In what is that Soma established?"
"In initiation. "But upon what is initiation established?
"Upon truth."
Therefore, they say to one who has been initiated, "Speak the truth," for initiation is established upon truth alone. But on what, then, is truth established?
"It is the heart," he said,
"for by the heart one knows the truth;
for in the heart alone does the truth become established."
"Even so, Yājñavalkya. "Even so, indeed, it is, Yājñavalkya. *Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad* 3.9.23.
"Which deity resides in this fixed quarter?
"The deity Agni. "In what is that Agni established?"
"Regarding speech:
on what, then, is speech established?
On the heart."
"On what, then, is the heart established? (Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad 3.9.24)
"O fool! said Yājñavalkya, "if you were to think this [Brahman] exists elsewhere than in us;
for if it were to exist elsewhere than in us, dogs would surely eat it, or birds would surely tear it apart."
"On what, then, are you and the self established?
"On the vital breath (prāṇa). "On what, then, is the vital breath established?"
"Apana. "In what, then, is apana established? "Vyana."
"In what, then, is the vyāna established?
"In the udāna. "In what, then, is the udāna established?"
"Equal," he said.
This very Self is "not this, not this.
It is ungraspable, for it cannot be grasped.
He is indestructible, for he is not destroyed; he is unattached, for he is not attached; he is unbound, for he does not tremble.
He is not harmed.
These eight bases are the eight worlds, the eight gods, and the eight persons.
Having withdrawn and then retracted those persons, he passed beyond them—that person of the Upaniṣads, I ask you about him.
"If you do not explain that to me, your head shall fall off.
Śākalya did not know it;
his head indeed fell off.
Even robbers carried off his bones, thinking them to be something else.
Then he said: "Venerable Brahmins, let whoever among you desires it question me; or let all of you question me.
Or, let me question whoever among you desires it; or let me question all of you."
Those Brahmins did not dare to do so.
He questioned them with these verses:
"As a tree is a great forest-plant, so is a person truly not false;
his body hairs are its leaves, and his outer skin is its outward bark. (Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad 3.9.28)
From his skin alone flows the blood; it is a scab from the skin.
Therefore, when that is pierced, the sap flows out, like [sap] from a struck tree.
Its flesh is the sapwood, its sinews the inner bark, and its bones the heartwood; the marrow within has been fashioned like marrow. (Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad 3.9.28)
When a tree is cut down, it grows again from its roots, even newer than before;
but when a mortal is cut down by death, from what root does he sprout forth?
"Do not say, 'From semen [it arises],' for that is born from the living one. A tree is indeed something that grows from a seed; its manifestation after death occurs immediately."
Just as a tree that they might uproot along with its roots would not come into being again,
from what root does a mortal man, once cut down by death, sprout forth?
Once born, he is not born again; who indeed could bring him to birth once more?
Consciousness, bliss, Brahman—the gift and the supreme goal of the giver.
He who is already born is not born again; who indeed could give birth to him once more?
Consciousness, bliss, Brahman—this is the supreme goal for the giver of gifts.
"For one who knows that and remains [in that state]," so it is said.
Janaka of Videha was sitting [in his assembly hall].
Then Yājñavalkya arrived.
He said to him: "Yājñavalkya, for what purpose have you come? Do you seek cattle, or do you seek subtle inquiries?"
"Both indeed, O Saṃrāj," he said. (Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad 4.1.1)
"Let us hear what someone has told you.
"Jitvan Śailini told me: 'Speech, indeed, is Brahman.
Just as one who possesses a mother, a father, and a teacher would speak, so did Śailini say: 'Speech, indeed, is Brahman.'"
"What would happen if one did not speak? [The other replied:
"But he told you its sphere and its foundation.
[The first asked: "He did not tell me."
"This, O Emperor, is but one quarter," he said.
"Tell us that, Yājñavalkya.
"Speech indeed is its abode, space its support; one should meditate upon it as intelligence (prajñā)."
"What is the state of wisdom, Yājñavalkya?
"Speech alone, O Emperor," he said.
"For by speech alone, O Emperor, a kinsman is recognized."

The Rigveda, Yajurveda, Samaveda, Atharvangirasa, history, ancient lore, sciences, Upanishads, verses, aphorisms, explanations, and commentaries; what is sacrificed, what is offered, what is eaten, and what is drunk; this world and the other world, and all beings—these, O Sovereign, are known through speech alone.
Speech, O Emperor, is indeed the supreme Brahman.
Speech does not desert him;
all beings flow toward him.
"Having become a god, he goes to the gods— he who, knowing this, worships it thus. "I shall give a thousand [cows] with an elephant and a bull," said Janaka of Videha.
Yājñavalkya said: "My father thought that one should not take [the teacher's fee] without having first instructed [the pupil]."
"Whatever anyone has told you, let us hear that.
"Udaṅka Śaulbāyana said to me:
'The vital breath (prāṇa) is indeed Brahman.'"
Just as one who has a mother, a father, and a teacher might say, so did Śaulbāyana speak: "Brahman is indeed prāṇa.
For what could there be for one who does not breathe? But he did not tell you its abode and its foundation.
"He did not tell me," [the king said].
"That was only one quarter, O Emperor," replied Yājñavalkya.
"Tell us that, Yājñavalkya! he requested.
"Life-breath (*prāṇa*) is the abode, space (*ākāśa*) is the foundation.
One should venerate this as 'the dear' (*priya*). "What is its dearness, Yājñavalkya?"
"Breath alone, O Emperor," he said.
"It is indeed for the sake of breath, O Emperor, that one causes an unworthy person to perform a sacrifice,
and accepts what ought not to be accepted."
Moreover, there arises even the fear of being killed in whatever direction one goes, O Emperor, solely for the sake of the vital breath (*prāṇa*).
The vital breath, O Emperor, is indeed the supreme Brahman;
the vital breath does not desert him.
All beings flow toward him;
having become a god, he goes to the gods—
he who, knowing this, meditates upon it.
"I shall give you a thousand cows with a bull as large as an elephant," said Janaka, the King of Videha.
Yājñavalkya replied, "My father believed that one should not accept a gift without having first given instruction."
"Let us hear what someone has told you.
"Barku Vārṣṇa told me:
'The eye, indeed, is Brahman.'"
"Just as one who has a mother, a father, and a teacher might say, so did that Vārṣṇa say: 'The eye, indeed, is Brahman.
For what would there be for one who does not see? But he did not tell you its abode and its support."
"He did not tell me," [the king said].
"That is but one quarter, O Emperor," [Yājñavalkya replied].
"Then do you tell us, Yājñavalkya."
"The eye itself is the abode; space is its foundation.
One should venerate this as 'Truth.
What, Yājñavalkya, is the nature of truth?"
"It is the eye itself, O Emperor," he said.
"For indeed, O Emperor, when they ask one who sees with the eye, 'Did you see?
and he says, 'I saw,' that becomes the truth."
"O Emperor, the eye is indeed the supreme Brahman.
The eye does not desert him;
all beings flow toward him."
"Having become a god, he goes to the gods— he who, knowing this, worships it thus. "I shall give a thousand [cows] with a bull as large as an elephant," said Janaka of Videha.
Yājñavalkya said: "My father thought that one should not take [the teacher's fee] without having first instructed [the pupil]."
"Let us hear what someone has told you.
"Bhāradvāja Gardabhīvipīta told me:
'The ear, indeed, is Brahman.'"
Just as one who has a mother, a father, and a teacher might say, so did Bhāradvāja speak: "The ear, indeed, is Brahman.
For what would there be for one who does not hear? But he did not tell you its abode and its support.
"He did not tell me," [the king said].
"That is but one quarter, O Emperor," [Yājñavalkya replied].
"Then do you tell us, Yājñavalkya."
"The ear indeed is the abode, space is its foundation; one should worship this as 'the infinite.
What is its infinity, O Yājñavalkya?
"The quarters themselves, O Emperor," he said.
Therefore, O Emperor, no matter which direction one travels, one never reaches its end;
for the directions are infinite. Indeed, O Emperor, the directions are the ear.
"The ear, O Emperor, is indeed the supreme Brahman.
The ear does not desert him;
all beings flow toward him."
"Having become a god, he goes to the gods— he who, knowing this, worships it thus. "I shall give a thousand [cows] with a bull as large as an elephant," said Janaka of Videha.
Yājñavalkya said: "My father thought that one should not take [the teacher's fee] without having first instructed [the pupil]."
"Whatever anyone has told you, let us hear that.
"Satyakāma Jābāla told me: 'The mind, indeed, is Brahman.
Just as one who possesses a mother, a father, and a teacher would speak, so did Jābāla say: 'The mind, indeed, is Brahman.'"
"What would happen to one who is mindless? "He told you its locus and foundation.
"He did not tell me," [Nārada said].
"This is but one quarter, O Emperor," he said.
"Tell us more, Yājñavalkya.
"The mind (*manas*) is its abode, space (*ākāśa*) is its foundation; one should worship it as bliss (*ānanda*)."
"What is the source of bliss (*ānanda*), Yājñavalkya?
"The mind itself, O Emperor," he said. "For by means of the mind, O Emperor, one approaches a woman; from her a son resembling himself is born. That is bliss."
"O Emperor, the mind indeed is the supreme Brahman.
The mind does not desert him;
all beings flow toward him."
"Having become a god, he goes to the gods— he who, knowing this, worships it thus. "I shall give a thousand [cows] with a bull as large as an elephant," said Janaka of Videha.
Yājñavalkya said: "My father thought that one should not take [the teacher's fee] without having first instructed [the pupil]."
"Whatever anyone has told you, let us hear that. "Vidagdha Śākalya told me:
'The heart, indeed, is Brahman.'"
"Just as one who has a mother, a father, and a teacher might say, so did Śākalya say: 'The heart, indeed, is Brahman.
For what could there be for one without a heart? [Yājñavalkya] replied, "But you have not told me its abode and its support."
"He did not tell me," [the king said].
"He told you only a single quarter, O Emperor," [Yājñavalkya replied].
"Then do you, Yājñavalkya, tell it to us."
"The heart is its abode, space is its foundation.
One should worship it as 'Stability' (sthitih). What is this stability, Yājñavalkya?"
"It is the heart indeed, O Emperor," he said.
"The heart, O Emperor, is the abode of all beings;
the heart, O Emperor, is the foundation of all beings."
For indeed, O Emperor, all beings are established in the heart alone.
The heart, O Emperor, is the supreme Brahman;
it does not abandon him.
All beings flow toward him;
having become a god, he goes to the gods—
he who, knowing this, meditates upon it.
"I shall give you a thousand cows with a bull as large as an elephant," said Janaka of Videha.
Yājñavalkya replied, "My father believed that one should not accept a gift without having first given instruction."
Janaka of Videha, descending from his seat of kusha grass, said: "Homage be to you, Yājñavalkya!
Teach me.
He replied: "Just as a king, O Emperor, about to set out on a long journey would prepare a chariot or a boat, even so have you prepared yourself with these secret doctrines (upaniṣads)."
"Thus, O Vṛndāraka, being wealthy, having studied the Vedas, and possessing the taught Upaniṣads, when you are released from here, where will you go?
"I do not know that, O Blessed One, where I shall go.
"Now, indeed, I shall tell you that where you shall go."
"Let the Blessed One speak," [he said]. Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad 4.2.1.
This person who is here in the right eye is indeed named Indha;
though he is Indha, they call him Indra by an indirect name, for the gods, as it were, love the indirect and dislike the direct. (Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad 4.2.2)
Now, this person-form in the left eye is his wife, Virāj;
their place of union is this space within the heart;
and their food is this lump of blood within the heart.
Now, their covering is this which is like a network within the heart. Now, their path for moving about is this channel that rises upward from the heart.
Just as a hair split a thousandfold, so these channels called *hitā* are established within the heart.
By means of these, indeed, this [subtle body] flows with the outflows;
therefore, it becomes, as it were, more secluded from food than this corporeal self.
Of him, the eastern direction is the forward vital breaths;
the southern direction is the rightward vital breaths;
the western direction is the backward vital breaths.
The northern direction is the upward vital breaths;
the upward direction is the upward vital breaths;
the downward direction is the downward vital breaths.
All directions are all vital breaths.
This very Self is "not this, not this.
It is ungraspable, for it cannot be grasped.
Unbreakable, for it is not broken; unattached, for it is not attached; unbound, it does not tremble.
"He does not perish.
Indeed, O Janaka, you have attained fearlessness," said Yājñavalkya.
Janaka of Videha replied, "May fearlessness come to you, O Yājñavalkya, you who, O Blessed One, have made us know fearlessness."
"Homage be to you!
These are the Videhas, and here am I," [he said]. (Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad 4.2.4)
Yājñavalkya went to Janaka of Videha, thinking,
"I shall have a discussion with him.
Now, it happened that Janaka of Videha and Yājñavalkya once conversed together regarding the Agnihotra sacrifice.
Yājñavalkya granted him a boon; he chose the right to ask any question he desired,
and Yājñavalkya granted it to him.
The Emperor himself was the first to question him.
"Yājñavalkya," he asked, "what is the light of this person?
"The sun is his light, O Emperor," he replied.
"By the light of the sun alone, he sits, moves about, performs his work, and returns."
"Even so, Yājñavalkya. "Even so, indeed, Yājñavalkya. Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad 4.3.2.
"When the sun has set, Yājñavalkya, what light does this person have?
"The moon indeed becomes his light.
"By the light of the moon alone, he sits, moves about, performs his work, and returns."
"Even so, Yājñavalkya. "So it is, Maitreyī. "This is indeed so, Yājñavalkya. Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad 4.3.3.
"When the sun has set, Yājñavalkya, and the moon has set, what light does this person have?
"Fire indeed becomes his light.
"With fire as his light, he sits, moves about, performs his work, and returns."
"Even so, Yājñavalkya. "So it is, Maitreyī. Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad 4.3.4.
"When the sun has set, Yājñavalkya, and the moon has set, and the fire has gone out, what light does this person have?
"Speech itself becomes his light," [he replied].
"By speech as his light, he sits, moves about, performs his work, and returns."

"Therefore, O Emperor, even where one's own hand is not discerned, or where speech rises up, there one simply returns [to the source]. It is just so, Yājñavalkya. "It is exactly so, Yājñavalkya. *Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad* 4.3.5.
"When the sun has set, Yājñavalkya, when the moon has set, when the fire has gone out, and speech has become silent, what light does this person have?
"The self alone becomes his light.
"By the light of the self alone, he sits, moves about, performs actions, and returns."
"What is the Self?"—it is this person consisting of consciousness, who is the light within the heart among the vital breaths.
Being the same [in both states], he wanders through both worlds; he meditates, as it were, and he stirs, as it were.
For, having become a dream, he transcends this world and the forms of death. (Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad 4.3.7)
Indeed, this person, when being born and entering a body, becomes united with evils;
when departing and dying, he leaves the evils behind.
For this very person, there are indeed only two states:
this world and the state of the other world;
the third is the intermediate state, the state of dream.
Abiding in that intermediate state, he beholds both states— this world and the state of the next world. Then,
according to the sequence he follows in the state of the next world, having traversed that sequence, he beholds both evils and joys.
When he falls asleep, taking a portion from this entire world, striking it out himself and creating it himself, he sleeps by his own radiance, by his own light;
here, this person becomes self-luminous.
There are no chariots there, no draft animals for chariots, and no roads;
yet he creates chariots, draft animals for chariots, and roads.
There are no joys, delights, or pleasures there; yet he creates joys, delights, and pleasures.
Then he creates joys, delights, and pleasures;
yet there are no pools, lotus ponds, or rivers there.
Then he creates pools, lotus ponds, and rivers.
For he is indeed the agent. (Br̥hadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad 4.3.10)
Regarding this, there are these verses:

"Having struck down the bodily [self] by means of dream-sleep, the Unsleeping One looks down upon those who sleep; taking the light, he returns again to his place—the golden person, the solitary swan. (Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad 4.3.11)
Protecting his lower nest with his vital breath, having moved outside the nest as an immortal,
that golden person, the solitary swan, goes wherever he desires as an immortal.
Moving through high and low states within the realm of dreams, the god creates many forms;
as if rejoicing with women, as if laughing, and even as if beholding terrors. *Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad* 4.3.13.
"They see his garden, yet no one sees him.
They say that one should not wake him while he is sleeping;
for it would be difficult to treat him who does not respond to it.
Moreover, they say: "This is indeed his place of waking;
for what he sees while awake, those same things he sees while asleep.
In this state, this person becomes self-luminous.
"Therefore, I give a thousand [cows] to the Blessed One. Speak further for the sake of liberation. ||| BrhUp_4.3.14 |||

Having rejoiced and wandered about in that state of serene confidence (*saṃprasāda*), and having seen both the auspicious and the inauspicious, he hastens back again according to the rule and according to his source, toward sleep itself.
Whatever he sees there, he remains untouched by it;
for this person is unattached.
"So it is, Yājñavalkya!
I give you a thousand [cows], O Blessed One.
Speak further for the sake of liberation alone."
Having enjoyed himself and wandered about in that dream, and having seen both good and evil, he hastens back again according to the rule and according to his source, toward the state of waking.
Whatever he sees there, he does not carry over with him;
for this person is unattached.
"So it is, Yājñavalkya.
I give you a thousand [cows], O Blessed One.
Speak further for the sake of liberation alone."

Having enjoyed himself and wandered about in this state of waking, and having seen both merit and evil, he hastens back again according to the rule, according to his source, toward the state of dream.
Just as a great fish swims along both banks, the near and the far, even so does this person move between these two states: the state of dream and the state of waking.

Just as in this space a hawk or a falcon, having flown about and become weary, folds its wings and remains poised for rest, even so does this person hasten toward that end, where, asleep, he desires no desire at all and sees no dream whatsoever. (Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad 4.3.19)
These, indeed, are his channels called *hitā*. They exist with a subtlety like that of a hair split a thousandfold.
They are filled with white, blue, brown, green, and red [fluids].
Now, when it seems as if they strike him, or conquer him, or as if an elephant chases him, or as if he falls into a pit;
Whatever fear one perceives while awake, that one imagines here through ignorance.
But when one imagines, "I am like a god, I am like a king; I indeed am all this," that is his highest world. (Br̥hadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad 4.3.20)
This, indeed, is his form that transcends all desire, free from evil, and fearless.
Just as a man embraced by a beloved wife knows nothing without nor within,
even so this person, embraced by the conscious Self (prājña ātman), knows nothing without nor within.
Now, this form of his is one in which all desires have been attained, whose desire is the Self alone, which is free from desire, and beyond sorrow.
In this state, the father becomes no-father, the mother no-mother; the worlds become no-worlds, the gods no-gods, and the Vedas no-Vedas.

Here, the thief becomes no-thief, the killer of an embryo no-killer of an embryo, the outcaste no-outcaste, the son of a degraded woman no-such, the Paulkasa no-Paulkasa, the ascetic no-ascetic, and the hermit no-hermit.
He is untouched by merit and untouched by evil.
For at that time, he has indeed crossed over all the sorrows of the heart.
Indeed, that which one does not see there, one does not see while seeing;
for there is no loss of the vision of the seer, because of its imperishability. But there is no second thing existing there, distinct from it, which one might see.
Indeed, when he does not smell, it is because, though smelling, he does not smell;
for there is no loss of the smeller's power of smelling, because of its imperishability. But there is no second thing, other than and distinct from him, that he might smell.
That which indeed does not taste, it is actually tasting even though it does not taste;
for there is no loss of the power of tasting in the taster, because of its imperishability.
But there is no second thing, other than that and separate from it, which it might taste.
Indeed, when one does not speak there, it is as if one were speaking even while not speaking;
for there is no loss of the speaker's power of speech, because of its imperishability.
Yet, there is no second thing there, other than that, distinct from it, which one might speak.
Indeed, that which he does not hear, he does not hear even while hearing;
for there is no loss of the hearing of the hearer, because it is indestructible.
But there is no second thing existing separate from him, other than himself, which he might hear.
Indeed, that which one does not think, while thinking, one does not think it;
for there is no loss of the thinker’s power of thought, because of its imperishability.
But there is no second thing, other than and distinct from it, which one might think. (Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad 4.3.28)
Indeed, he does not touch that which is touched; though touching, he does not touch it.
For there is no destruction of the toucher’s power of touching, because of his imperishability.
But there is no second thing existing apart from him, distinct from him, which he might touch.
That which he does not perceive, he indeed perceives even while not perceiving it;
for there is no loss of the perceiver’s power of perception, because it is indestructible.
But there is no second thing, other than and distinct from him, that he might perceive. (Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad 4.3.30)

Or rather, where there is something else as it were, there one might see another, one might smell another, one might taste another, one might speak another, one might hear another, one might think of another, one might touch another, and one might perceive another. (Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad 4.3.31)
"He becomes one with water, a seer, non-dual.
This, O Emperor, is the world of Brahman.
Thus did Yājñavalkya instruct him.
This is his supreme goal;
this is his supreme attainment;
this is his supreme world.
This is his supreme bliss;
all other beings subsist on a mere fraction of this very bliss.
That which is the supreme bliss of humans is the case of one who has attained success and prosperity among men, who is the lord of others, and who is most fully endowed with all human enjoyments.
Now, a hundredfold the bliss of humans is equal to a single bliss of the ancestors who have won their worlds.
Now, a hundredfold the bliss of the ancestors who have won their worlds is equal to a single bliss in the world of the Gandharvas.
Now, a hundredfold the joys in the world of the Gandharvas are equal to one joy of the gods by action— those who attain divinity through their ritual acts.
Now, a hundredfold the joys of the gods by action are equal to one joy of the gods by birth,
and also to that of a learned Śrotriya who is free from evil and untouched by desire.
Now, a hundredfold the blisses of those born as gods (ājānadeva) constitute one bliss in the world of Prajāpati—
for such is the case for one who is learned in the Vedas (śrotriya), free from evil, and unassailed by desire.
And a hundredfold the blisses in the world of Prajāpati constitute one bliss in the world of Brahman.
And he who is a learned scholar of the Vedas, free from crookedness, and unassailed by desire— this indeed is the supreme bliss;
this, O Emperor, is the world of Brahman.
Thus spoke Yājñavalkya:
"I give a thousand [cows] to you, O Blessed One.
Speak further only for the sake of liberation."
At this point, Yājñavalkya became afraid, thinking: "This wise king has excluded me from all [the topics of] inquiry. Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad 4.3.33.

Having enjoyed himself and wandered about in that state of dream, and having seen both good and evil, he hastens back again, according to the rule and according to his origin, toward the waking state itself.
Just as a well-lubricated cart might go along creaking, even so this bodily self, mounted by the conscious self (prājña-ātman),
goes along creaking when he becomes one who breathes heavily upward.
When he comes to this attenuation— whether through old age or through illness—
and reaches a state of attenuation, then, just as a mango, a fig, or a pipal fruit is released from its stalk,
even so this person, being completely released from these limbs, hastens back again according to his direction and according to his source, for the sake of vital breath alone.
Just as when a king approaches, the fierce enforcers of law, the charioteers, and the village headmen prepare food, drink, and lodging for him, thinking, "He is coming! He is arriving!";
even so, all beings prepare for one who knows this, thinking, "Brahman is coming! Brahman is arriving!"
Just as when a king is about to depart on a journey, his fierce executioners, charioteers, and village headmen gather around him,
even so at the time of death all the vital breaths gather around this self,
at which time one becomes one whose breath moves only upward.
When this self reaches weakness and falls, as it were, into a state of confusion,
then these vital breaths (prāṇas) gather around it.
Taking up these particles of light, it descends into the heart itself.
When this person who consists of the eye turns away from there,
then he becomes one who no longer knows forms.
"They become one and do not see," they say; "they become one and do not smell," they say; "they become one and do not taste," they say.
"It becomes one and does not speak," they say; "it becomes one and does not hear," they say; "it becomes one and does not think," they say.
They say it becomes one and does not touch;
they say it becomes one and does not cognize.
Then, the tip of this very heart flashes forth.
By that light, this self departs—
either through the eye, or from the head, or from other parts of the body.
As it departs, the vital breath (prāṇa) follows after it.
When the vital breath departs, all the vital breaths depart after it;
he becomes possessed of consciousness and enters into that very consciousness.
Knowledge and action follow after him, as does his prior wisdom.

Just as a caterpillar, having reached the end of a blade of grass, takes hold of another support and draws itself toward it, even so this Self, having cast off this body and caused ignorance to depart, takes hold of another support and draws itself toward it. (Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad 4.4.3)
Just as a weaver takes a measure of cloth and weaves another form that is newer and more beautiful,
even so this self, having cast off this body and dispelled ignorance, fashions another form that is newer and more beautiful—
whether it be the form of a parent, a Gandharva, a god, Prajāpati, Brahmā, or of other beings.

This very Self is indeed Brahman, consisting of consciousness, consisting of mind, consisting of breath, consisting of sight, consisting of hearing, consisting of earth, consisting of water, consisting of air, consisting of space, consisting of fire, consisting of what is not fire, consisting of desire, consisting of what is not desire, consisting of anger, consisting of what is not anger, consisting of dharma, consisting of adharma, and consisting of everything.
Thus, as to this [teaching] that "one consists of this world, one consists of the other world":
according as one acts and according as one conducts oneself, so does one become;
by performing good deeds one becomes good.
An evildoer becomes evil;
one becomes meritorious through meritorious action, and evil through evil action.
Furthermore, they say:
"This person consists entirely of desire. "As is his desire, so is his resolve; as is his resolve, so is the deed he performs."
Whatever action one performs, that one attains.
Regarding this, there is this verse:
"Clinging to that very thing, he goes with his karma and his subtle body (liṅga) to where his mind is attached.
Having reached the end of that karma, whatever he does here—"
"From that world he returns again to this world for the sake of action"—
thus it is for one who still desires. But for one who does not desire— who is without desire, free from desire, whose desire is fulfilled, whose desire is the Self— his vital breaths do not depart.
Being Brahman indeed, he merges into Brahman.
Regarding this, there is this verse:
"When all desires that dwell within his heart are released, then the mortal becomes immortal; he attains Brahman even here."
Just as the slough of a snake might lie dead and cast away upon an anthill,
even so does this body lie;
but this bodiless, immortal life-breath is indeed Brahman, it is indeed radiance.
"Therefore, I give a thousand [cows] to the Blessed One," said Janaka of Videha.
Regarding this, there are these verses:
"The path is subtle, broad, and ancient; it has been touched by me and discovered by me alone.
By it, the wise who know Brahman go from here upwards to the heavenly world, liberated. (Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad 4.4.8)
Of that path they say it is white, or blue, tawny, green, and red.
This is the path discovered by Brahmā; by it goes the knower of Brahman, the doer of good deeds, and the man of radiant luster.
Into blind darkness enter those who worship ignorance;
into a darkness even greater than that, as it were, enter those who delight in knowledge.
"Blissless indeed are those worlds, shrouded in blind darkness;
to them go after death those people who are ignorant and lacking in wisdom. (Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad 4.4.11)
If a person were to know the Self as "This am I," desiring what, or longing for what, would he suffer in accordance with the body? (Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad 4.4.12)

He who has discovered and awakened to the Self that has entered this body, so difficult to penetrate and dense—He is the maker of all, for He is the creator of everything; His is the world, and He alone is the world itself. (Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad 4.4.13)
"Only here do we exist; indeed, we know this. If we did not know it, there would be a great destruction.
Those who know it become immortal, while others enter only into suffering. (Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad 4.4.14)
When one perceives this Self directly as the divine Lord of what has been and what is to be, one does not shrink away from it.
Since the year revolves with the days, therefore the gods worship that light of lights as life and immortality. (Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad 4.4.16)
In whom the five classes of beings and space are established—him alone I consider the Self; knowing him as the immortal Brahman, I am immortal.
Those who know the breath of breath, the eye of the eye, the ear of the ear, and the mind of the mind—they have perceived the ancient, supreme Brahman. (Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad 4.4.18)
It is to be perceived by the mind alone; there is no diversity whatsoever here. He who perceives diversity here goes from death to death. (Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad 4.4.19)
This immeasurable, eternal reality is to be perceived as one alone.
Stainless, beyond space, unborn, the Self, great and firm.
Having understood that very [Self], the wise Brahmin should practice wisdom;
he should not ponder over many words, for that is a weariness of speech. (Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad 4.4.21)
This indeed is that great unborn Self, who consists of consciousness among the vital breaths;
he lies within that space which is inside the heart.
He is the ruler of all.
He is the lord of all,
the sovereign of all;
he does not become greater by good action.
He is certainly not inferior because of what is unwholesome;
he is the Lord of All,
he is the Sovereign of Beings.
This is the guardian of beings;
this is the bridge, the support for these worlds so that they may not be confounded.
Brahmins seek to know this very one through the recitation of the Vedas, through sacrifice, through giving, through austerity, and through fasting.
Having known this very thing, one becomes a sage;
desiring this very world, mendicants go forth into the homeless life.
This very point is expressed by a Rigvedic verse:
"This is the eternal greatness of a Brahmin: he does not increase by action, nor does he become smaller. Having known the path of that [Self] alone, one is not stained by evil action."
Therefore, one who knows this, having become calm, self-controlled, withdrawn, patient, and concentrated, sees the Self in the very Self;
he sees everything as the Self.
Evil does not overcome him.
He crosses over all evil;
evil does not afflict him;
he afflicts all evil.
"Free from evil, stainless, and free from doubt, one becomes a Brāhmaṇa.
This, O Emperor, is the world of Brahman;
you have reached it," said Yājñavalkya.
"Therefore, I give the Videhas to the Blessed One, and myself as well, along with my daughter."
Verily, this great unborn Self is the eater of food and the giver of wealth;
he who knows this finds wealth. *Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad* 4.4.24.
Verily, this great unborn Self is ageless, undying, immortal, fearless Brahman.
Brahman is indeed fearless. Verily, he who knows this becomes the fearless Brahman. (Br̥hadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad 4.4.25)
Now, Yājñavalkya had two wives, Maitreyī and Kātyāyanī.
Of these two, Maitreyī was a seeker of Brahman,
while Kātyāyanī at that time possessed only the common wisdom of women.
Then Yājñavalkya, wishing to adopt another mode of life, [spoke].
"Maitreyī," Yājñavalkya said,
"I am indeed about to depart from this state.
Come, let me make a final settlement for you with this Kātyāyanī."
Maitreyī said:
"If, O Venerable Sir, this entire earth were filled with wealth for me, would I thereby become immortal, or not?
"No," said Yājñavalkya.
Just as is the life of those who possess material means,
so indeed would your life be;
but there is no hope for immortality through wealth.
Maitreyī said:
"What should I do with that by which I would not become immortal?
Tell me only that which you know, O Venerable One."
Yājñavalkya said:
"Truly, you have increased what is dear to us, since you are dear to us. Come now."
"This is so; I shall explain it to you.
But while I am explaining, reflect deeply upon it. (Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad 4.5.5)

He said: "Indeed, my dear, it is not out of love for the husband that the husband is dear; rather, it is out of love for the Self that the husband is dear. Indeed, my dear, it is not out of love for the wife that the wife is dear; rather, it is out of love for the Self that the wife is dear."

Verily, it is not out of love for their sons that sons are dear, but it is out of love for oneself that sons are dear. Verily, it is not out of love for wealth that wealth is dear, but it is out of love for oneself that wealth is dear.
Verily, it is not out of love for cattle that cattle are dear, but it is out of love for oneself that cattle are dear.

"Verily, it is not for the sake of the Brahmin that the Brahmin is dear; rather, it is for the sake of the Self that the Brahmin is dear. Verily, it is not for the sake of the Kṣatriya that the Kṣatriya is dear; rather, it is for the sake of the Self that the Kṣatriya is dear.
Verily, it is not for the sake of the worlds that the worlds are dear; rather, it is for the sake of the Self that the worlds are dear."
Truly, it is not for the sake of the gods that the gods are dear; rather, it is for the sake of the Self that the gods are dear.

Truly, it is not for the sake of the Vedas that the Vedas are dear; rather, it is for the sake of the Self that the Vedas are dear. Truly, it is not for the sake of beings that beings are dear; rather, it is for the sake of the Self that beings are dear.
"Verily, it is not for the sake of all that all becomes dear, but for the sake of the Self, Maitreyī, all becomes dear.
Verily, the Self, Maitreyī, is to be seen, heard, reflected upon, and meditated upon.
When the Self, verily, is seen, heard, reflected upon, and known, all this is known. (Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad 4.5.6)
Brahman abandons him who knows the Vedas as other than the Self; the Kṣatra abandons him who knows the Kṣatra as other than the Self;
the worlds abandon him who knows the worlds as other than the Self.
The gods desert him who knows the gods as other than the Self;
the Vedas desert him who knows the Vedas as other than the Self;
the beings desert him who knows the beings as other than the Self.
He who knows all this as other than the Self is abandoned by all that.
This is Brahman, this is the Kṣatra, these are the worlds, these are the gods, these are the Vedas, these are all beings—all this is what this Self is. (Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad 4.5.7)
Just as, when a drum is being beaten, one would not be able to grasp the external sounds; but by grasping the drum, or the striking of the drum, the sound is grasped. (Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad 4.5.8)
Just as when a conch is being blown, one cannot grasp the external sounds;
yet by grasping the conch, or the blower of the conch, the sound is grasped.
Just as, when a lute is being played, one would not be able to grasp the external sounds;
but by grasping the lute, or the lute-player, the sound is grasped. (Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad 4.5.10)

Just as from a fire of damp wood that has been kindled, various clouds of smoke issue forth, even so, my dear, the Rigveda, Yajurveda, Samaveda, Atharvangirasa, history, ancient lore, sciences, Upanishads, verses, aphorisms, explanations, commentaries, the sacrificed, the offered, and the eaten— this is the breath of this great Being.
This world and the next world, and all beings—these are all merely his breaths. (Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad 4.5.11)
Just as the ocean is the single point of convergence for all waters,
so the skin is the single point of convergence for all tactile sensations; so the two nostrils are the single point of convergence for all odors.
In this way, the tongue is the single point of convergence for all tastes; in this way, the eye is the single point of convergence for all forms;
in this way, the ear is the single point of convergence for all sounds.
Thus, the mind is the single point of convergence for all volitions;
thus, the heart is the single point of convergence for all branches of knowledge;
thus, the two hands are the single point of convergence for all actions.
In this way, the organ of generation is the single point of convergence for all pleasures;
in this way, the anus is the single point of convergence for all excretions;
in this way, the feet are the single point of convergence for all paths.
In this way, speech is the single point of convergence for all the Vedas.
Just as a block of salt has no interior and no exterior, but is entirely a mass of flavor, even so, my dear,
this Self has no interior and no exterior, but is entirely a mass of consciousness.
Arising from these elements, it passes away back into them.
"There is no consciousness after death," O Āre, I say;
thus spoke Yājñavalkya. *Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad* 4.5.13.
Maitreyī said:
"Right here, my lord, you have landed me in utter confusion;
indeed, I do not understand this."
He said: "Verily, I do not speak delusion to you.
This Self, indeed, is indestructible and its nature is such that it is not subject to perishing. (Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad 4.5.14)
For where there is, as it were, duality, there one sees another;
there one smells another;
there one tastes another.
Then one speaks to the other; then one hears the other;
then one thinks of the other; then one touches the other.
Therefore, one person knows another.

But where for him everything has become the Self alone, then by what and whom should he see? Then by what and whom should he smell? Then by what and whom should he taste? Then by what and whom should he speak? Then by what and whom should he hear? Then by what and whom should he think? Then...
By what could one touch whom? By what could one perceive whom?
By what could one perceive that by which one perceives all this?
That very Self is "not this, not this."
It is ungraspable, for it cannot be grasped; it is indestructible, for it cannot be destroyed; it is unattached, for it is not attached.
"Unattached, he is not shaken and does not suffer.
By what, my dear Maitreyī, should one know the Knower? Having thus spoken this instruction—"This much indeed, my dear, is immortality"—Yājñavalkya departed. *Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad* 4.5.15.
Now, the lineage: Pautimāṣya from Gaupavana; Gaupavana from Pautimāṣya.
Pautimāṣya from Gaupavana;
Gaupavana from Kauśika;
Kauśika from Kauṇḍinya.
Kauṇḍinya from Śāṇḍilya;
Śāṇḍilya from both Kauśika and Gautama;
and Gautama.
From Agniveśya; Agniveśya from Gārgya;
Gārgya from Gārgya.
Gārgya from Gautama; Gautama from Saitava;
Saitava from Pārāśaryāyaṇa.
Pārāśaryāyaṇa from Gārgyāyaṇa;
Gārgyāyaṇa from Uddālakāyana;
Uddālakāyana from Jābālāyana.
Jābālāyana from Mādhyandināyana;
Mādhyandināyana from Saukarāyaṇa;
Saukarāyaṇa from Kāṣāyaṇa.
Kāṣāyaṇa from Sāyakāyana; Sāyakāyana from Kauśikāyani;
Kauśikāyani from [Gautama].
From Ghṛtakauśika; Ghṛtakauśika from Pārāśarya;
Pārāśarya from Pārāśarya.
Pārāśarya from Jātukarṇya; Jātukarṇya from both Āsurāyaṇa and Yaska;
and Āsurāyaṇa from Traivaṇi.
Traivaṇi from Aupajandhani;
Aupajandhani from Āsuri;
Āsuri from Bhāradvāja.
Bhāradvāja from Ātreya;
Ātreya from Māṇṭi;
Māṇṭi from Gautama.
Gautama [received it] from Gautama;
Gautama from Vātsya;
Vātsya from Śāṇḍilya.
Śāṇḍilya [received it] from Kaiśorya Kāpya;
Kaiśorya Kāpya from Kumāraharita;
and Kumāraharita from Gālava.
Gālava from Vidarbhīkauṇḍinya; Vidarbhīkauṇḍinya from Vatsanapād Bābhrava;
Vatsanapād Bābhrava from Pathas Saubhara.
Panthāḥ Saubhara received it from Ayāsya Āṅgirasa;
Ayāsya Āṅgirasa from Ābhūti Tvaṣṭra;
Ābhūti Tvaṣṭra from Viśvarūpa Tvaṣṭra.
Viśvarūpa, the son of Tvaṣṭṛ, [received it] from the Aśvins;
the Aśvins [received it] from Dadhyañc Ātharvaṇa; Dadhyañc Ātharvaṇa [received it] from Atharvan Daiva.
Atharvan Daiva [received it] from Prādhvaṃsana Mṛtyu; Prādhvaṃsana Mṛtyu from Prādhvaṃsana;
and Prādhvaṃsana from Ekarṣi.
Ekarṣi from Viprajitti;
Viprajitti from Vyaṣṭi;
Vyaṣṭi from Sanāru.
Sanāru from Sanātana;
Sanātana from Sanaga;
Sanaga from Parameṣṭhin.
Parameṣṭhin is Brahman;
Brahman is the Self-existent.
Salutation to Brahman.
That is full, this is full; from the full, the full is drawn forth.
When the full of the full is taken away, the full alone remains.
Space is Brahman.
"Space is ancient;
the wind is space," so indeed said Kauravyāyaṇīputra.
The Brahmins know this as the Veda; by means of this, that which is to be known is known.

Three groups of Prajāpati’s offspring— gods, humans, and asuras— lived the life of a religious student under their father Prajāpati. Having completed their studentship, the gods said, "May your honor speak to us."
To them he spoke this syllable: "Da. He asked, "Have you understood? They replied, "We have understood."
"Do you say, 'Be self-controlled'? "Yes," he replied, "I have understood. 5.2.1.
Then the men said to him, "May your honor speak to us.
To them he spoke this very syllable: "Da. [They asked: "Did you understand? [He replied: "Yes."
"We understood," they said. "You told us, 'It has been given. "Yes," he said, "you understood. (Br̥hadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad 5.2.2)
Then the Asuras said to him, "May your honor speak to us.
To them he spoke this very syllable: "Da. [They asked: "Did you understand? [He replied: "Yes."
"We have understood," they said. "Did you say 'Have compassion'?
"Yes," he replied, "I understood."
This very same divine voice, the thunder, repeats it: "Da-da-da"—that is, "Be self-controlled (damyata), give (datta), be compassionate (dayadhvam).
Therefore, one should practice these three: self-control, giving, and compassion.
This heart is Prajāpati;
it is Brahman;
it is all.
This very thing is the three-syllabled "Heart" (hṛdayam).
"Hṛ" is one syllable.
Both his own people and others bring [offerings] to him who knows thus.
"Da" is one syllable;
both his own people and others give to him who knows this.
"Yam" is one syllable.
He who knows this goes to the heavenly world. *Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad* 5.3.1.
That indeed was this very thing;
it was truth alone.
He who knows this great, first-born being as "Brahman is Truth" wins these worlds—indeed, that [other world] is already won by him—who thus knows this great, first-born being.
"The Vedas know that Brahman is truth;
for truth indeed is Brahman. (Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad 5.4.1)
In the beginning, this world was indeed only water. That water created the Real (satya).
The Real is Brahman.
Brahmā [created] Prajāpati; Prajāpati [created] the gods;
those gods worship truth alone.
This consists of three syllables: *sa*, *ti*, and *yam*. *Sa* is one syllable; *ti* is one syllable;
*yam* is one syllable.
The first and the last syllables are truth; in between is falsehood.
This falsehood is enclosed on both sides by truth;
it thus becomes nothing but truth.
Untruth does not harm one who knows thus.
That which is the Truth is yonder sun;

it is the person who is in this orb and the person who is here in the right eye. These two are established in one another: he is established in this [body] by means of his rays, and this [person] is established in yonder [sun] by means of the vital breaths (*prāṇa*).
When he is about to depart, he sees this orb as pure;
these rays do not return to him.
Of that person who is in this orb, "bhūḥ" is the head;
the head is one, and this syllable is one.
"Bhuvaḥ" is the arms.
The two arms are these two syllables;
"Svar" is the support;
the two supports are these two syllables.
Its secret name (upaniṣad) is "Day.
He who knows this destroys evil and leaves it behind. Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad 5.5.3.
This person who is in the right eye—his head is "bhūḥ";
there is one head, and this is one syllable.
His arms are "bhuvaḥ."
The two arms are these two syllables;
*svar* is the support;
the two supports are these two syllables.
Its secret name (upaniṣad) is "I.
He who knows this slays evil and is liberated from it. (Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad 5.5.4)
This person consists of mind; he is composed of light and is truth.
Within him, in the heart, he is like a grain of rice or a grain of barley.
He is the lord of all, the sovereign of all, and he rules over all this, whatever exists. (Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad 5.6.1)
"Lightning is Brahman," they say.
It is called lightning because it flashes (*vidāna*). He who knows that "lightning is Brahman" flashes away his evils.
For Brahman is indeed lightning. *Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad* 5.7.1.
One should worship speech as a cow.
It has four udders:
the utterance "svāhā," the utterance "vaṣaṭ," the utterance "hanta," and the utterance "svadhā."
Of her two breasts, the gods subsist on two:
the utterance *svāhā* and the utterance *vaṣaṭ*; human beings [subsist] on the utterance *hanta*.
The ancestors have the utterance *svadhā* as their food;
of that [cow], the breath is the bull and the mind is the calf.
This is Agni Vaiśvānara, who is within the person; by him this food is digested,
which is what is eaten here.
This is its sound which one hears when one covers the ears;
when he is about to depart, he does not hear that sound.
When indeed a person departs from this world, he goes to the wind; for him, the wind parts there as the hole of a chariot wheel,
and by that opening he ascends upward.
He comes to the sun;
for him,
it opens there like the aperture of a drum.
By that [path], he ascends upwards;
he reaches the moon;
there, for him, it opens up.
Just as the sound of a drum [pervades] the sky,
by that he ascends upward;
he comes to the world that is free from sorrow and free from disease.
In him he dwells for eternal years.
This indeed is the supreme austerity: when one who is emaciated undergoes penance.
He who knows this conquers the supreme world.
This indeed is the supreme austerity: when they carry the deceased to the forest.
He who knows this indeed conquers the highest world.
This is indeed the highest austerity: when they place the deceased upon the fire;
he who knows this indeed conquers the highest world. (Br̥hadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad 5.11.1)
"Some say that food is Brahman;
but that is not so,
for food putrefies without life."
"Breath is Brahman," say some;
that is not so,
for breath indeed withers without food.
Indeed, these two deities, having become one, attain the supreme state.
Regarding this, Prātṛda once said to his father:
"What good could I possibly do for one who knows this? And what evil could I possibly do to him?"
He said, "Do not [speak thus], Pāṇin Māprātṛda!
Who among these two, having become a single entity, attains supremacy? To him he then spoke this: "Vī."
Food indeed is *vi*; for in food all these beings are entered (*viṣṭa*). "Ram."
The vital breath (prāṇa) is indeed delight (ram).
For in the vital breath all these beings delight;
indeed, all beings enter into it.
All beings find delight in him who knows this. *Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad* 5.12.1.
The *uktha*. The *uktha* is indeed the vital breath (*prāṇa*), for the vital breath raises up all this.
From this, the hero who knows the hymns rises up; he who knows this wins union with the hymn and residence in the same world as it. Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad 5.13.1.
The Yajus. The vital breath (prāṇa) is indeed the Yajus; for in the vital breath all these beings are joined together.
