All beings strive for his preeminence; he who knows this wins union with and residence in the same world as the Yajus. Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad 5.13.2.
Sāman. Breath indeed is the sāman; for in breath all these beings are united (samyañci).
All beings truly strive for his preeminence;
he who knows this wins union with and residence in the same world as the Sāman. Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad 5.13.3.
The ruling power (kṣatra).
The vital breath (prāṇa) is indeed the ruling power;
for the vital breath is indeed the ruling power.
Prāṇa protects him from injury;
he attains sovereign power and food.
He who knows this wins union with and residence in the same world as sovereign power (kṣatra). Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad 5.13.4.
"Earth, intermediate space, and heaven"—these are eight syllables.
Now, one foot of the Gāyatrī indeed consists of eight syllables;
this [triad] is indeed that [foot] of hers.
As far as these three worlds extend, so far indeed does he conquer who knows this very foot of hers thus.
The *ṛc*s, the *yajus* formulas, and the *sāman*s—these are eight syllables. Indeed, one foot of the *gāyatrī* consists of eight syllables; this very thing constitutes that foot of hers.
As great as this threefold knowledge is, so much indeed does he conquer who knows this foot of it thus.
"Prāṇa, apāna, vyāna"—these are eight syllables.
Indeed, one foot of the Gāyatrī consists of eight syllables;
this very [foot] of hers is that.
As far as this living world extends, so far indeed does he conquer who knows this foot of hers thus.
Now, this is her fourth, visible foot, which is beyond the dust—that which shines yonder.
For that which is fourth is indeed the "fourth" (*turīya*).
"The visible step"—for he is, as it were, visible;
"beyond the dust"—for he indeed shines higher and higher above all the dust.
Thus indeed does one shine with splendor and fame who knows this step of his in this manner.
This very Gāyatrī is established upon that fourth, visible foot, beyond the dust of the atmosphere;
and that, indeed, is established upon Truth.
The eye, indeed, is Truth.
The eye, indeed, is truth. Therefore, if two people should come here at present disputing, one saying "I saw" and the other saying "I heard," we would side with him who says "I saw."
Therefore, let us have faith in that alone. That truth is indeed established upon strength; and strength, verily, is the vital breath (prāṇa).
That is established in breath;
therefore they say, "Strength is more excellent than truth.
Thus, indeed, this Gāyatrī is established in the self (adhyātma).
This very [earth] is that which supports the *gayas*; the vital breaths (*prāṇa*) are indeed the *gayas*;
thus, it supports the vital breaths.
Because he protected (*tatre*) the vital breaths (*gaya*) therein, it is therefore called *gāyatrī*. That which he recites as the *sāvitrī* is indeed this very same one;
by reciting it for someone, he protects that person's vital breaths.
Some recite this very Sāvitrī as an Anuṣṭubh verse, saying: "The Anuṣṭubh is speech;
thus we recite it as speech."
One should not do so;
one should rather recite the Gāyatrī Sāvitrī itself.
For even if one who knows this should receive much in the way of gifts, it does not equal even a single foot of the Gāyatrī.

If one were to receive these three worlds filled to their capacity, he would obtain only this first foot of her. Furthermore, if one were to receive as much as there is of the triple knowledge (*trayī vidyā*), he would obtain this second foot of her.
Furthermore, if one were to receive as many living beings as exist here, he would obtain this third foot of her.
Now, this very fourth, the visible foot, which shines yonder beyond the dust—
that is not to be attained by anyone at all;
how then could one receive so much?
Its worship:
"Gāyatrī, you are one-footed, two-footed, three-footed, four-footed; you are footless."
For you do not fall away. Homage to your fourth, visible foot, which is beyond the realm of dust!
"May that [person] over there not reach me! [he says].
Or,
if one should say, "May this desire of his not be fulfilled," that desire of his is indeed not fulfilled for whomsoever he thus pays homage, or if he says, "I have attained that."
Janaka of Videha said this to Buḍila Āśvatarāśvi: "Since you, sir, claimed to be a knower of the Gāyatrī, how is it that you have become an elephant and are carrying [me]?
He replied, "For I did not know its mouth, O King."
Fire indeed is its mouth.
For even if one throws much fuel into the fire, it completely consumes it all;
in the same way, even if one who knows this performs much evil, he completely consumes it all and becomes pure, cleansed, ageless, and immortal.
The face of truth is covered by a golden vessel;
O Pūṣan, uncover it for me, who am devoted to the law of truth, so that I may see.
O Pūṣan, sole seer, Yama, Sūrya, son of Prajāpati, spread out your rays and withdraw your splendor.
That form of yours which is most beautiful, that I behold; that person who is there, I am he.
Vāyu is the breath, the immortal; and this body ends in ashes. Om! O Kratu, remember; remember what was done. O Kratu, remember; remember what was done.
O Agni, lead us by a good path to wealth, O God who knows all ways;
remove from us the sin that leads astray; we shall offer you the most abundant speech of homage.
Verily, he who knows the oldest and the best becomes the oldest and the best among his own people.
Breath indeed is the oldest and the best;
he becomes the oldest and the best among his own people.
Moreover, he prospers with those for whom he desires to prosper—he who knows this thus. (Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad 6.1.1)
He who knows the most excellent (*vasiṣṭhā*) indeed becomes the most excellent among his own people. Speech, indeed, is the most excellent. He becomes the most excellent among his own people.
Moreover, he prospers for whomsoever he desires to prosper, provided that person knows this. Br̥hadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad 6.1.2.
He who knows the foundation indeed stands firm on level ground;
he stands firm on difficult terrain.
The eye, verily, is the foundation.
For with the eye one stands firm on both even ground and difficult terrain;
he stands firm on even ground and stands firm on difficult terrain who knows this. *Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad* 6.1.3.
Verily, he who knows attainment—for him that desire which he desires is attained.
The ear, indeed, is attainment;
for in the ear all these Vedas are fully contained.
Whatever desire he may desire, it is fulfilled for him who knows this. (Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad 6.1.4)
Verily, he who knows the abode becomes an abode for his own people and an abode for other men.
The mind, indeed, is the abode;
one becomes an abode for his own people and an abode for other men.
He who knows thus. Br̥hadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad 6.1.5.
He who knows procreation indeed procreates with offspring and cattle. Semen, verily, is procreation.
He indeed procreates with offspring and cattle.
Whoever knows this thus. Br̥hadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad 6.1.6.

These vital breaths, disputing among themselves as to who was the best, went to Brahmā. They said to him: "Which of us is the most excellent? He replied: "He among you, upon whose departure this body is considered the worst, he is the most excellent of you."
Speech departed.
Having been away for a year, it returned and said, "How were you able to live without me?
They replied, "We lived just as people do who do not speak with speech, but breathe with the breath, see with the eye, hear with the ear, know with the mind, and procreate with semen; thus we lived."
Speech indeed entered.
The eye departed.
Having stayed away for a year, it returned and said, "How were you able to live without me?

They replied, "Just as the blind, though not seeing with the eye, lived by breathing with the breath, speaking with speech, hearing with the ear, knowing with the mind, and procreating with semen—thus we lived."
The eye indeed entered.
The ear departed.
Having stayed away for a year, it returned and said, "How were you able to live without me?

They replied, "Just as the deaf—though not hearing with the ear—live by breathing with the breath, speaking with speech, seeing with the eye, knowing with the mind, and procreating with semen; even so have we lived."
It entered the ear. Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad 6.1.10.
The mind departed.
Having stayed away for a year, it returned and said: "How were you able to live without me?
They replied: "Just as ignorant, deluded people breathe with the breath, speak with speech, see with the eye, hear with the ear, and procreate with semen—even so did we live."
The mind entered. Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad 6.1.11.
The semen departed.
Having stayed away for a year, it returned and said, "How were you able to live without me?
They replied, "Just as eunuchs live without procreating—breathing with the breath, speaking with speech, seeing with the eye, hearing with the ear, and knowing with the mind—even so have we lived."
It entered as semen.
Then, as the vital breath was about to depart, just as a great Sindh horse might tear up its foot-tethers and pegs, even so did it tear these vital functions apart.
They said: "O Venerable One, do not depart!
We shall certainly not be able to live without you."
"Offer an oblation to me," he said.
"So be it," they replied. (Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad 6.1.13)
Then Speech said: "Insofar as I am the most excellent (*vasiṣṭha*), you are that most excellent;
insofar as I am the foundation (*pratiṣṭhā*), you are that foundation"—thus spoke the Eye. "Insofar as I am attainment (*saṃpat*), you are that attainment"—thus spoke the Ear.
"Or, 'What I am as a locus, that you are as a locus'—this is the mind.
Or, 'What I am as procreation, that you are as procreation'—this is semen. What is my food? What is my clothing?"
"Whatever there is here, down to dogs, down to worms, down to insects and moths—that is your food; water is your clothing.
Indeed, for one who knows this food of food, no food has been eaten that is not fit to be eaten, nor has anything been accepted that is not fit to be accepted.
Knowing this, learned Vedic scholars sip water before eating and sip water after eating;
they consider this to be making that very food non-naked.
Śvetaketu Āruṇeya came to the assembly of the Pañcālas. He approached Pravāhaṇa Jaibali while he was being waited upon by his attendants. Seeing him, [Pravāhaṇa] addressed him, saying: "Young man!"
He replied, "Yes, sir. [The father said,] "Have you been instructed by your father? He said, "Yes, sir.
(Br̥hadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad 6.2.1)
"Do you know how these creatures, when they depart, diverge?
"No," he said.
"Do you know how they return again to this world?"
"No," he replied, "do you know how it is that this world is not filled up, even though many people go there again and again? "No," he replied.
"Do you know at which oblation, when it has been offered, the waters, having assumed human voices, rise up and speak?
"No," he replied.
"Do you know the entrance to the path of the gods or the path of the fathers?"
By performing which [deeds], people set out upon either the path of the gods (*devayāna*) or the path of the fathers (*pitṛyāṇa*).
For indeed, we have heard the word of the Seer:
"I have heard of two paths—of the fathers and of the gods, as well as of mortals."
"Into these two, this entire moving world comes together—that which is between the father and the mother.
"I do not know even one of them," he said. (Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad 6.2.2)
Then he invited him to stay for the night;
disregarding the invitation to stay, the youth ran away.
He went to his father.
He said to him: "Is it not the case, sir, that you have previously spoken to us as those who are instructed? How so, Sumedhas?
[Sumedhas replied: "A kinsman of the royal class asked me five questions."
Then he does not perceive even a single thing.
"Which are they? [the son asked]. "These," he replied, citing the [senses] as examples. (Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad 6.2.3)
He said: "My dear, you should know us thus: whatever I know, all that I have told you.
But go there;
having approached him, we two shall live the life of a religious student."
"You yourself should go.
Gautama went to where Pravāhaṇa Jaibali was.
Having offered him a seat, he brought water for him.
Then he offered him the guest-offering (arghya). He said to him, "We grant a boon to the venerable Gautama."
He said: "This boon has been promised to me;
however, tell me that word which you spoke in the presence of the boy. Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad 6.2.5.
He said: "Gautama, those [boons] are indeed among the divine;
speak for the human ones."
He said: "It is well known that I have already received much gold, cattle, horses, female slaves, attendants, and clothing.
May you not, sir, be one who diminishes what is for us so great, endless, and boundless.
"Then, Gautama, seek it through the proper channel," he replied.
"I am approaching you," he said. Formerly, they used to approach [a teacher] merely by word of mouth;
thus he dwelt there, proclaiming his arrival as a pupil.

He said: "In this way, O Gautama, neither you nor your ancestors have committed an offense against us, since this knowledge has never before dwelt with any Brahmin. Nevertheless, I shall impart it to you."
"For who would be fit to refuse you when you speak thus? (Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad 6.2.8)
That world, O Gautama, is indeed the fire;
its fuel is the sun,
and its smoke is the rays.
The day is its flame;
the quarters are its embers;
the intermediate quarters are its sparks.
In this very fire, the gods offer faith as an oblation;
from that oblation, King Soma comes into being.
"Or rather, O Gautama, Agni is Parjanya;
his fuel is the year itself,
and his smoke is the clouds."
The lightning is its flame; the thunderbolt is its embers;
the thunderclaps are its sparks.
Into this very fire, the gods offer King Soma;
from that oblation, rain comes into being.
"This world, indeed, is the fire, O Gautama;
its fuel is the earth, and its smoke is fire."
The night is its flame;
the moon is its embers;
the stars are its sparks.
Into this very fire, the gods offer rain;
from that oblation, food comes into being.
"Or rather, O Gautama, man is the fire. His opened mouth is the fuel;
his breath is the smoke."
Speech is the flame;
the eye is the embers;
the ear is the sparks.
Into this very fire the gods offer food;
from that oblation, semen comes into being.
Woman, indeed, is the fire, O Gautama; her lap is the kindling,
and her body hair is the smoke.
The womb is the flame;
what one does within it are the embers;
the delights are the sparks.
Into this very fire the gods offer semen; from that oblation a person comes into being. He lives as long as he lives.
Now, when one dies— Br̥hadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad 6.2.13.
Then they carry him to the fire;
for him, the fire itself becomes the fire; the fuel becomes the fuel.
Smoke, smoke;
flame, flame;
embers, embers.
"Scintillations, scintillations! Into this very fire the gods offer the person. From that oblation, the person of radiant color comes into being. (Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad 6.2.14)
Those who know this thus, and those who, in the forest, venerate truth through faith—they pass into the light;
from the light, into day;
from day, into the waxing fortnight.
From the fortnight of the waxing moon, during those six months that the sun moves northward,
[the soul goes] from the months to the world of the gods,
and from the world of the gods to the sun.
From the sun [they go] to the lightning. A person consisting of mind (mānasa-puruṣa) approaches those who are of the lightning and leads them to the worlds of Brahman.
There, in those worlds of Brahman, they dwell as the highest among the highest.
For them there is no returning again.
Now, those who win the worlds through sacrifice, charity, and austerity reach the smoke;
from smoke they reach the night;
from the night, the waning fortnight.
From the waning fortnight, during those six months that the sun moves southward,
[the sacrificer goes] from the months to the world of the fathers,
and from the world of the fathers to the moon.
Having reached the moon, they become food.
There, the gods consume them in the same manner as they do King Soma, saying, "Swell up! Wane away!
When that [consumption] of theirs comes to an end, they emerge into this very space.
From space, wind;
from wind, rain;
from rain, earth.
Having reached the earth, they become food;
they are then offered into the fire of man, and from there they are born in the fire of woman. Rising up toward the worlds, they revolve in this very same way.
Now, those who do not know these two paths become worms, moths, and whatever is biting.

He who should desire, "May I attain greatness," should, during the northern course of the sun, on an auspicious day of the waxing moon, having observed the *upasad* vow for twelve days, collect all kinds of herbs and fruits in a vessel made of *udumbara* wood— either a bronze cup or a wooden bowl. Having swept around the site, smeared it with cow-dung,
established the fire, strewn grass around it, and prepared the clarified butter according to the prescribed ritual, he should, under a male asterism, mix the mash and offer it as an oblation.
O Jātavedas, as many gods as dwell within you who strike down the desires of a man from every side—to them I offer this portion; may they, being satisfied, satisfy me with all my desires, svāhā!
You who lie across, saying, "I am the supporter."
With a stream of clarified butter, I worship you, the one who brings about fulfillment; Svāhā! BrhUp_6.3.1.
Having offered in the fire with "To the eldest, svāhā! To the best, svāhā! he pours the residue into the mash.
Having offered in the fire with "To the breath, svāhā! To the most excellent, svāhā! he pours the residue into the mash.
Having offered in the fire with "To speech, svāhā! To the foundation, svāhā! he pours the residue into the mash.
Having offered into the fire with "To the eye, svāhā! To prosperity, svāhā!", he pours the remnants into the mash.
Having offered into the fire with "To the ear, svāhā! To the abode, svāhā!", he pours the remnants into the mash.
Having offered into the fire with "To the mind, svāhā! To progeny, svāhā!", he pours the remnants into the mash.
Having offered an oblation into the fire with the words, "To the seed, svāhā!", he pours the remnants into the mash.
Having offered an oblation into the fire with "Svāhā to Agni," he pours the residue into the mash.
Having offered an oblation into the fire with "Svāhā to Soma," he pours the residue into the mash.
Having offered an oblation into the fire with "Bhūḥ Svāhā," he pours the residue into the mash.
Having offered an oblation into the fire with "Bhuvaḥ svāhā," he pours the residue into the mash.
Having offered an oblation into the fire with "Svaḥ svāhā," he pours the residue into the mash.
Having offered an oblation into the fire with "Bhūr bhuvaḥ svaḥ svāhā," he pours the residue into the mash.
Having offered an oblation into the fire with "Svāhā to Brahman," he pours the remnants into the mash.
Having offered an oblation into the fire with "Svāhā to Kṣatra," he pours the remnants into the mash.
Having offered an oblation into the fire with "Svāhā to Bhūta," he pours the remnants into the mash.
Having offered an oblation into the fire with "To Bhaviṣya, svāhā!", he pours the remnants into the mash.
Having offered an oblation into the fire with "To Viśva, svāhā!", he pours the remnants into the mash.
Having offered an oblation into the fire with "To Sarva, svāhā!", he pours the remnants into the mash.
Having offered an oblation into the fire with the words, "To Prajāpati, svāhā!", he pours the residue into the mash.
Then he touches it, saying: "Thou art whirling; thou art flaming;
thou art full."
You are the proffered;
you are the single assembly;
you are the uttered *hiṅ*.
You are being uttered with the sound *hiṃ*;
you are the *udgītha*;
you are being sung as the *udgītha*.
You have been made to hear;
you have been made to respond;
you are moist yet ablaze.
You are pervasive;
you are powerful;
you are food.
"You are light; you are the finale; you are the absorber. (Br̥hadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad 6.3.4)
Then he lifts it up with the words: "O raw one, raw indeed is thy greatness;
for he is the King, the Ruler, the Overlord.
May he make me the King, the Ruler, the Overlord. (Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad 6.3.5)
Then he sips it with:
"That excellent glory of Savitṛ;
honeyed are the winds for the one who follows the cosmic order; honeyed do the rivers flow."
May the plants be sweet for us.
Bhūḥ Svāhā!
We meditate upon the splendor of the divine.
May the night be honey-sweet, and may the dawn be honey-sweet; may the earthly realm be honey-sweet, and may our father, heaven, be honey-sweet.
Svāhā! Bhūḥ! Svāhā!
May he who shall impel our thoughts [be gracious].
May the Lord of the Forest be honey-sweet for us; may the Sun be honey-sweet;
may the cows be honey-sweet for us.

He recites "Svaḥ svāhā! and the entire Sāvitrī verse; he recites all the honey-verses and finally, "May I become this All—bhūr bhuvaḥ svaḥ svāhā! Having sipped water and washed his hands, he lies down behind the fire with his head toward the east.
In the morning, he worships the sun:
"You are the unique lotus among the quarters;
may I become the unique lotus among men."
Having returned by the same way he came and sitting behind the fire, he mutters the lineage formula (vaṃśa).

Having taught this very [doctrine] to his pupil Vājasaneya Yājñavalkya, Uddālaka Āruṇi said: "Even if one were to pour it onto a withered stump, branches would grow and leaves would sprout. Having taught this very same thing to his pupil Madhuka Paiṅgya, Vājasaneya Yājñavalkya said: "Even if one were to pour it onto a withered stump, branches would grow and leaves would sprout."

Madhuka Paiṅgya, having taught this very same thing to his pupil Cūla Bhāgavitti, said: "Even if one were to pour it onto a dry stump, branches would spring up and leaves would grow. And Cūla Bhāgavitti, having taught this very same thing to his pupil Jānaki Āyaḥsthūṇa, said: "Even if one were to pour it onto a dry stump, branches would spring up and leaves would grow."
Jānaki Āyasthūṇa, having told this very thing to his pupil Satyakāma Jābāla, said: "Even if one were to pour this on a dry stump, branches would grow and leaves would sprout.
And Satyakāma Jābāla, having told this very thing to his pupils, said: "Even if one were to pour this on a dry stump, branches would grow and leaves would sprout.
One should not tell this to anyone who is not a son or a pupil. (Br̥hadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad 6.3.12)
There are four items made of udumbara wood:
a sruva ladle of udumbara, a camasa cup of udumbara, a fuel-stick of udumbara, and two churning-sticks of udumbara.
There are ten kinds of cultivated grains.
Rice, barley, sesame, beans, fine millet, wheat, lentils, chickpeas, and vetches—he grinds them and pours them into curds, honey, and ghee;
he offers them as an oblation of clarified butter. BrhUp 6.3.13.
Of these beings, the earth is the essence;
of the earth, water;
of water, plants.
From herbs come flowers;
from flowers come fruits;
from fruits comes man.
The seed of the person. Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad 6.4.1.
Prajāpati reflected: "Come now, I shall provide a foundation for him. He created a woman.
Having created her, he approached her from below.
Therefore, one should approach a woman from below.
He brought this pressing-stone forward from his own self and discharged it at her.
Her lap is the sacrificial altar; her body hair is the sacred grass;
her skin is the two pressing-boards.
Kindled in the middle, those two are the testicles.

Indeed, as great as the world becomes for the sacrificer who performs the Vājapeya sacrifice, so great a world becomes for him who, knowing this, engages in sexual intercourse with these women; he appropriates the merit of those women.
Now, if one who does not know this engages in sexual intercourse, his women take away his merit.
Knowing this, Uddālaka Āruṇi indeed said this;
knowing this, Nāka Maudgalya indeed said this;

and knowing this, Kumārahārita indeed said: "Many young men of the Brāhmaṇa caste, lacking vital power and deprived of merit, depart from this world when they do not know this and engage in sexual intercourse below."
Regarding the phrase "they move":
much of this semen is discharged, whether one is asleep or awake.
He should touch it or recite over it the mantra: "That semen of mine which today has spilled upon the earth, which has flowed into the plants, or into the waters—this semen I take back up again.
May my virility return to me; may my splendor return; may my fortune return."
"Furthermore, may the fires and the hearths be arranged according to their proper places.
Having said this, he should take [the ashes] with his ring finger and thumb and wipe them away either between the breasts or between the eyebrows.
Now, if he should see his own reflection in water, let him address it with the mantra: "In me be splendor, sensory power, fame, wealth, and merit.
Indeed, she who has washed away her impurities is the very embodiment of the Fortune (*Śrī*) of women;
therefore, one should approach and address a woman of such renown who has washed away her impurities.
If she should not give it to him, he may, at his will, purchase her from her.
If she should still not give it to him, he may, at his will, strike her with a stick or with his hand and pass by her, saying:
"I take away your vigor and your glory."
He indeed becomes ill-reputed. Br̥hadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad 6.4.7.
If she should give it to him, [he should say]: "With my faculty, I bestow glory upon your glory.
Thus both become glorious.
If he should desire her—wishing, "May she be mine"—he should fix his intent upon her, join mouth to mouth, touch her private parts, and mutter:
"From limb by limb you arise, from the heart you are born; you are the essence of the limbs. Intoxicate this woman for me, as one might intoxicate a poisoned arrow. (Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad 6.4.9)
Now, if one should desire of a woman, "May she not conceive," he should, after having performed the ritual act with her, join his mouth to her mouth and first exhale and then inhale, saying:
"By my organ and seed, I take away your seed. She indeed becomes seedless.
Now, if he should desire of a woman, "May she conceive," he should place his purpose in her, join mouth to mouth, and exhaling, he should inhale [upon her], saying:
"With my faculty and with my seed, I place seed in you.
She indeed becomes pregnant.

Now, if one should hate a man who has a paramour with his wife, he should kindle a fire in an unbaked earthen vessel, spread out reed-grass as sacrificial litter with its points turned backward, and into that [fire] he should offer these reed-arrows, smeared with clarified butter and with their points turned backward,
[saying]: "In my kindled fire you have sacrificed!"
"I take your out-breath and in-breath, O so-and-so! "In my kindled fire you have offered [evil]! I take away your sons and cattle, O so-and-so!"
"You have sacrificed in my kindled fire; I take from you [the merit of] that sacrifice and good deed, O so-and-so! "You have sacrificed in my kindled fire!"
"O you two, space and the quarters, take him away!"—thus he says.
Indeed, that man whom a Brahmin who knows this curses departs from this world deprived of his senses and stripped of his merit.
Therefore, one who knows this should not seek to joke with the wife of a learned Śrotriya.
For indeed, one who knows this becomes supreme.
Now, if one should find his wife in her menses, she shall not drink from a bronze vessel for three days;
she shall remain in unwashed garments.
Neither a *vṛṣala* nor a *vṛṣalī* woman shall touch her.
At the end of three nights, having bathed, he should have the rice grains pounded.

If one should desire, "May a fair son be born to me; may he recite the Veda and reach a full lifespan," they should cook rice with milk and eat it with clarified butter; thus they will be capable of procreating. (Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad 6.4.14)

Now, if one should desire: "May a son be born to me who is tawny and reddish-brown, may he study the two Vedas, and may he live his full span of life," they should have curd-rice cooked with clarified butter and eat it; thus they will be capable of procreating such a child. (Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad 6.4.15)

Now, if one should desire: "May a son be born to me who is dark-complexioned and red-eyed, who shall master the three Vedas and live his full span of life," then, having cooked rice with ghee, they two should eat it; they will be able to procreate such a child.
Now, if one should desire, "May a learned daughter be born to me, and may she live her full span of life," they should cook rice mixed with sesame seeds and eat it with clarified butter;
thus they will be able to procreate [such a child].

Now, if one should desire: "May a son be born to me who is wise, renowned, capable in assembly, a speaker of words that are well-received, who shall master all the Vedas and live his full span of life," they should cook meat-rice with clarified butter and eat it;
thus they will be able to procreate.
With the meat of a bull or a ram.

Then, early in the morning, having performed the rites for the *sthālīpāka* and prepared the clarified butter, he offers a portion of the *sthālīpāka* with the formula: "To Agni, svāhā! To Anumati, svāhā! To the god Savitṛ of true impulsion, svāhā!
Having offered and taken out [the remainder], he eats it;
having eaten, he gives the other [portion] to his wife.

Having washed his hands and filled a water-vessel, he sprinkles her with it three times, saying: "Arise from here, O Viśvāvasu; seek another woman who is more favorable. Be united with a husband in this wife. (Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad 6.4.19)
Then he approaches her: "I am he (ama), you are she (sā). You are she, I am he.
I am the Sāman, you are the Ṛc."
"I am the sky, you are the earth. Come, let us two unite; let us together deposit the seed for the sake of obtaining a male son. (Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad 6.4.20)
Then he causes her thighs to part with the words, "May Heaven and Earth separate.
Having positioned himself upon her and joined mouth to mouth, he strokes her three times in the direction of the hair with the mantra:
"May Viṣṇu prepare the womb; may Tvaṣṭṛ fashion the forms."
May Prajāpati sprinkle [the seed]; may Dhātṛ place the embryo within you.
O Sinīvālī, bestow an embryo; O broad-hipped one, bestow an embryo.
May the two divine Aśvins, wreathed with lotuses, bestow an embryo upon you.
The two fire-sticks are made of gold, from which the Aśvins churned [the fire].
That embryo of yours we invoke for birth in the tenth month;
as the earth has Agni as its embryo, as the sky is pregnant with Indra.
"As the wind is the embryo of the quarters, so do I place an embryo within you, O [Name]! Thus he says.
He sprinkles her who is about to give birth with water:
"As the wind stirs a lotus pond on every side, so let your embryo stir; let it come forth together with the afterbirth."
"This stall has been made for Indra, secured with a bolt and enclosed on all sides;
O Indra, destroy it with the embryo within, along with the Sāvarṇas! (Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad 6.4.23)

When [the son] has been born, having kindled the fire, having placed him on his lap, and having poured the speckled butter (pṛṣadājya) into a bronze vessel, he offers portions of the speckled butter, saying:
"May I thrive in this man's own house, may a thousand prosper for me; may he not cut me off from his proximity in offspring and cattle—svāhā!"

"I offer my vital breaths into you with my mind; svāhā! Whatever I have overdone in this rite, or whatever I have done here deficiently—may Agni Sviṣṭakṛt, the wise one, make that well-offered and well-sacrificed for us; svāhā! (Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad 6.4.24)
Then, having placed [his mouth] close to his right ear, he says "Speech! Speech! three times.
Then, having mixed together curds, honey, and ghee, he makes him eat it with a piece of gold held against [the mixture], saying:
"I place *bhūḥ* in you; I place *bhuvaḥ* in you; I place *svaḥ* in you; *bhūr bhuvaḥ svaḥ*, I place everything in you."
Then he gives him a name, saying, "You are Veda.
This indeed becomes his secret name.

Then, having handed him over to his mother, he gives her the breast with [the mantra]: "O Sarasvatī, that breast of yours which is inexhaustible, which is refreshing, which bestows jewels, which finds wealth, which is a good giver, and by which you nourish all desirable things—that one, bring here for him to suck. (Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad 6.4.27)
Then he addresses his mother: "Ilā, daughter of Mitra and Varuṇa, you have given birth to a hero among heroes;
may you become possessed of heroes, she who has made us possessed of heroes.
Regarding him, they say: "O, you have truly become a father beyond [the ordinary]!"
"Truly, you have become our great-grandfather!
You have indeed reached the highest pinnacle in prosperity, fame, and Vedic splendor, since a son has been born to a Brahmin who knows such things. (Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad 6.4.28)
Now, the lineage: Pautimāṣīputra from Kātyāyanīputra;
Kātyāyanīputra from Gautamīputra.
Gautamīputra [was the son] of Bhāradvājīputra;
Bhāradvājīputra [was the son] of Pārāśarīputra;
Pārāśarīputra [was the son] of Aupasvastīputra.
Aupasvastīputra from Pārāśarīputra; Pārāśarīputra from Kātyāyanīputra;
Kātyāyanīputra from Kauśikīputra.
From Kauśikīputra, from Ālambīputra, and from Vaiyāghrapadīputra.
Vaiyāghrapadīputra [is descended] from Kāṇvīputra and from Kāpīputra. Kāpīputra... BrhUp 6.5.1.
From Ātreyīputra; Ātreyīputra from Gautamīputra;
Gautamīputra from Bhāradvājīputra.
Bhāradvājīputra [received it] from Pārāśarīputra; Pārāśarīputra from Vātsīputra;
and Vātsīputra from Pārāśarīputra.
Pārāśarīputra from Vārkāruṇīputra; Vārkāruṇīputra from Vārkāruṇīputra;
Vārkāruṇīputra from Ārtabhāgīputra.
Ārtabhāgīputra from Śauṅgīputra; Śauṅgīputra from Sāṅkṛtīputra;
Sāṅkṛtīputra from Ālambāyanīputra.
Ālambāyanīputra [is descended] from Ālambīputra;
Ālambīputra from Jāyantīputra;
Jāyantīputra from Māṇḍūkāyanīputra.
Māṇḍūkāyanīputra [received it] from Māṇḍūkīputra;
Māṇḍūkīputra from Śāṇḍilīputra;
Śāṇḍilīputra from Rāthītarīputra.
Rāthītarīputra from Bhālukīputra;
Bhālukīputra from two Krauñcikīputras;
the two Krauñcikīputras from Vaidabhṛtīputra.
Vaidabhṛtīputra from Kārśakeyīputra;
Kārśakeyīputra from Prācīnayogīputra;
Prācīnayogīputra from Sāñjīvīputra.
Sāñjīvīputra [received it] from Prāśnīputra Āsurivāsina; Prāśnīputra from Āsurāyaṇa;
Āsurāyaṇa from Āsureḥ.
Āsuri. Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad 6.5.2.
From Yājñavalkya; Yājñavalkya from Uddālaka; Uddālaka from Aruṇa.
Aruṇa from Upaveśi; Upaveśi from Kuśri;
Kuśri from Vājaśravas.
Vājaśravas from Jīhvāvat Bādhyoga; Jīhvāvat Bādhyoga from Asita Vārṣagaṇa;
Asita Vārṣagaṇa from Harita Kaśyapa.
Harita Kaśyapa from Śilpa Kaśyapa;
Śilpa Kaśyapa from Kaśyapa Naidhruvi;
Kaśyapa Naidhruvi from Vāk.
Speech came from Ambhiṇī;
Ambhiṇī from Āditya.
These white Yajus formulas are proclaimed by Vājasaneya Yājñavalkya, who is descended from Āditya.
The lineage is the same up to Sañjīvīputra; Sañjīvīputra [received it] from Māṇḍūkāyani;
Māṇḍūkāyani from Māṇḍavya.
Māṇḍavya from Kautsa;
Kautsa from Māhitthi;
Māhitthi from Vāmakakṣāyaṇa.
Vāmakakṣāyaṇa from Śāṇḍilya;
Śāṇḍilya from Vātsya;
Vātsya from Kuśri.
Kuśri from Yajñavacas Rājastambāyana;
Yajñavacas Rājastambāyana from Tura Kāvaṣeya;
Tura Kāvaṣeya from Prajāpati.
Prajāpati [is born] from Brahman;
Brahman is self-existent.
Salutation to Brahman!
